why.say: Quick game: Better Question. I've written two questions on the board, and you vote with your hands. Question one: “Was it because you had no car?” Question two: “What, if anything, made it hard to get seen sooner?” Hands up for one. Hands up for two. {name}, you voted for one, so defend it for ten seconds. Here's the reveal. Question one gets you a yes. Question two gets you the truth. The only gap explanation that holds up against an adjuster is John Doe's own explanation, in his own words, backed by paper you can check: a work schedule, a doctor's availability note, a receipt. Your job is to draw it out and write it down exactly as he says it. You don't explain it for him, defend it or judge it. And here's the teaser: by the end of this block, I'll show you how one friendly sentence on this call can hand the defense their whole argument.
why.ask: {name}, which of those two questions would the defense lawyer rather you asked John Doe, and why?

theory.say: Here's the road for the gap interview, in plain words. You plan your questions, never the answers you expect. You open on the record with the date, your role and his consent to record. You ask open questions and follow his words. You ask for the paper. You read his story back to him. And you write it down, with a dated task for every document he mentions. Underneath sits one rule: coordinate, don't commingle. That just means the medical side and the legal side don't get mixed up in your notes. You write facts, never conclusions, because your opinion in a note is something the defense can use. Now, TV has ruined us a little. On TV, the detective pounds the table and the witness cracks. On this job, the detective asks a soft open question, then shuts up and types. {name}, which one do you think actually gets the truth?
theory.ask: {name}, why is staying quiet after an open question harder than it sounds?

frame.say: Let's bring back A-C-T, because the gap interview lives inside it. A-C-T is our three-step plan the minute something goes wrong in care: Assess, Coordinate, Track. Before I walk it, {name}, guess: is a gap in treatment a medical danger or a legal danger? Hold it. Assess comes first. A medical danger, like a fever or a screw coming loose after surgery, goes to the doctor today. A legal danger, like a gap or a vague note, goes to Atty. Thorne. And the answer: a gap is a legal danger. Then Coordinate: you call the provider's office to clarify, and you clear whatever barrier the client names, whether it's rides, scheduling or a referral. Track means you write down the flag and every fix you tried that same day. Then back to monitoring, where the question is always: is the plan working? The lazy version flags it and forgets it. The high-value version flags it, fixes the barrier, and checks back in.
frame.ask: {name}, looking at John Doe's file right now, which step of A-C-T is his 14-Day Gap sitting in?

rules.say: Here are the rules for the gap call. You investigate; you don't advocate. Read the EMS report, the 02/20/2026 urgent-care history and the timeline, then write a plan that holds questions only. Run a funnel: broad open questions first, follow-ups built on his words, and short yes-or-no questions last, only to pin a date or a document. Never lead, and never judge. You know the usual reasons, like rides, co-pays and work schedules, but you never offer them. Record only with his spoken consent. If Keystone wants a Recorded Statement, which is the insurance company taping his version of events, he declines and sends them to us. Confirm his 03/05/2026 consult with Dr. Reyes, and ask how he'll get to care once the rental ends 03/19/2026. Now the friendly sentence I promised: “Don't worry, the gap won't matter.” Sounds kind. It's legal advice. Reassure the process, never the outcome. And when a client says “I was busy,” that's not an explanation, that's a chapter title. Your next question is “busy with what?”
rules.ask: {name}, if John Doe's reason is true anyway, why does it matter how you asked for it?

model.say: Have a look at this board, and before I explain it, {name}, read me the first green line and the first red line out loud. Thank you. On the left, in green, it says ask it open. On the right, in red, never like this. Every open question sits on the same line as the leading version it replaces, so you can read straight across and hear the difference. That last red row has a little UPL tag on it. UPL means the unauthorized practice of law, giving legal advice when you're not a lawyer, and that row is the soothing line: kind on the surface, an opinion on his case underneath. Down below is the funnel: first open, then follow his words, then pin the dates and documents. And notice the pill at its mouth: recorded, consent on the record. Same fact, asked two ways, produces two different cases. The lazy call asks the red column fast. The high-value call asks the green column slow.
model.ask: {name}, reading across the rows, which red question do you think you'd be most tempted to ask on a real call?

job.say: Now let's follow this on the job. It starts when the records show the 14-day gap. You read the EMS report, the urgent-care history and the treatment timeline in the CMS, and you save your question plan in Case Notes before the call, with no question in it naming a reason. When the call connects in the Call Simulator with AI John Doe, you state the date, who's on, and that it's recorded, and you get his consent and confirm he's somewhere private. I once had a client take this call from a packed barbershop, with three guys chiming in on what really happened. Privilege, which keeps our talk with the client protected, doesn't love an audience. If he asks what the gap does to his case, no opinion; log it and send it to Atty. Thorne through Tasks the same day. Why does all this care matter? Because months from now, the adjuster will read the gap and try to knock thousands off the offer. A clean, documented explanation is what keeps that money on the table.
job.ask: {name}, where in that sequence do you think a nervous new Case Manager is most likely to slip?

dodont.say: Time for 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues one at a time, and as soon as you think you've got it, call Do or Don't and name the rule behind it. A right call scores a point. {name}, you keep score; {name}, you're first up. The good habits: asking open, following his words and closing last, reading his story back so he can correct you, and preventing the next gap now, which is far cheaper than explaining a second one in the demand. The traps: a question that names the reason you expect, blaming him for the gap, and soothing. “Don't worry” is the most common UPL slip in this module. Now your mystery for the next lesson. The adjuster is going to say this gap proves John Doe healed. Somewhere on his file is a piece of paper, made before anyone was thinking about a claim, that says otherwise. {name}, find it before I show it.
dodont.ask: {name}, what's the difference between telling John consistent care matters and telling him what this gap does to his case?

why.say: Hands up if you've ever ghosted someone. Come on, a friend, a dentist, a gym that kept calling. Keep them up. Now keep them up if you felt a little guilty about it. Right. Clients ghost us too, and almost never because they're bad people. They're in pain, they're overwhelmed, they changed phones. And when you finally do get a text back, it says new phone, who dis. That's not a client, that's a plot twist. So here's my teaser: this lesson isn't about chasing a client. It's about something sneakier. When a client goes quiet, the case keeps running without them. The deadlines don't stop. The No Contact Protocol, which is just our step-by-step plan for when a client stops answering, does three jobs. It tracks the silence officially, it proves the firm tried hard before anyone talks about ending the case, and it protects the firm if somebody later asks, what did you do? {name}, I'll tell you which of those three jobs matters most in a minute. Make your guess now.
why.ask: {name}, if John Doe went quiet tomorrow, who gets hurt if nobody can prove what the firm did to reach him?

theory.say: Here's the road, in plain words. First you look inside the file before you call anyone: the case status, the deadlines, the last time we spoke. Then you reach out, and you climb a ladder: two phone calls, then email and text, then the emergency contact, then a certified letter, which is mail where the post office gives us proof it was delivered. Then you tell Atty. Thorne what the silence puts at risk. A few words you'll hear. Due diligence just means proof we made a real, reasonable effort, written down. Approved channels are the ways the client agreed at intake we could contact them, and only those count. And the emergency contact is the backup person who can still reach the client. Now, guess who that is on John Doe's file. {name}? It's Margaret Doe, his mother. Remember that name. She becomes very important in about ten minutes.
theory.ask: {name}, where on John Doe's file would you look to find his approved contact channels?

frame.say: Before I show you this list, {name}, a quick bet: do clients go silent out of nowhere, or is there usually a warning sign? Hold that. Here's the reveal: silence almost always starts with a bottleneck, which is just a spot where the work slows down or gets stuck. Missing information, like a wrong phone number or no incident details. Slow follow-up, where we asked a question and nobody chased the answer. A Conflict Check, the search to make sure we don't already represent the other side, stuck in a backlog. Intake forms with wrong dates or missing signatures. Facts so unclear the attorney has to review them. And plain old communication gaps between departments. The lazy Case Manager says the client went dark. The high-value Case Manager asks, what did we do that made it easy for them to drift? Every one of these bottlenecks makes the eventual demand weaker, because a gap on our side looks like a gap in the case.
frame.ask: {name}, looking at John Doe's file right now, which of these bottlenecks do you think he's closest to?

rules.say: Here are the rules, and here's the habit that separates the pros. Step 1 is internal review: check the status, the live deadlines and the last contact date before you dial. Everybody wants to skip it. Step 2 is the ladder: at least two phone calls, then email and text, then the emergency contact, then certified mail or a formal letter. And this is the one people fail. You climb by channel, not by volume. The lazy version is calling the same cell number nine times and writing tried everything. Bonus points if his voicemail box was full the whole time, so you basically left nine messages for a robot that says the mailbox is full. The high-value version is two calls, then an email, then a text, then Margaret, each logged with date, time, channel and outcome, and a follow-up reminder set. Step 3 is telling Atty. Thorne, because deadlines don't pause for silence. And the line: you can tell the client what we need and by when. You can't tell them we're dropping their case.
rules.ask: {name}, before you pick up the phone, what deadline is already running on John Doe's file?

model.say: Here's the whole protocol on one picture, and there's a little hidden lesson in how it's drawn. Down the left is a spine of six stations. The first three are in full colour: internal review, contact attempts and team notification. That's today. Stations four to six are greyed out with a next lesson tag. On the right, station two opens into a ladder of channels: phone, then email and text, then the emergency contact, then certified mail. Now look closely. {name}, what do you notice about the size of the rungs? Each one gets wider. That's the hidden lesson: every step up reaches further and costs more effort, so you don't skip rungs and you don't stand on one rung forever. And down in the corner, the red card: the statute of limitations, the legal deadline to file the lawsuit, keeps running the whole time.
model.ask: {name}, why do you think each rung on that ladder is drawn wider than the one above it?

job.say: Let me tell you how this plays out for real. A Case Manager I trained once logged eleven calls to a silent client in two days. Eleven. She was so proud. Turns out the client had dropped his phone in a lake while fishing. Every one of those calls went to the bottom of the lake. One email would have reached him in an hour. So here's the job. John Doe misses an appointment. That's your trigger. You open the Case Summary in the CMS and do Step 1 so you know the live deadlines. Then you work the ladder in the Communications Log, the file's diary of every contact, each attempt logged with date, time, channel and outcome. When the ladder's done, you escalate to Atty. Thorne through Tasks with the impact spelled out: the SOL of 02/06/2028 and any hearing dates. Why it matters: an adjuster who sees a client vanish assumes the injuries weren't that bad. Our log is how we prove otherwise.
job.ask: {name}, what would Atty. Thorne need to see in that escalation before acting on it?

dodont.say: Game time: 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I reveal one clue at a time. The moment you know where it's going, shout Do or Don't and name the rule. First one to get it right three times wins bragging rights for the day. {name}, you're on the buzzer first. Some rounds are good habits, like setting a follow-up reminder the second a request goes out, or giving the client an easy way to answer: a call window, a text, an upload link. Some are traps, like letting a file sit with nothing logged because we're waiting on the client, or blaming the client for what's really our own process gap. And listen hard for channel versus volume, the one people miss most. Now your mystery for the next activity: John Doe's file has two calls to his mobile on the phone system and zero entries in the log. {name}, figure out what that missing log costs us.
dodont.ask: {name}, why does calling Margaret count as a new channel when a third call to John's mobile doesn't?

why.say: Quick game: would you rather spend five hundred dollars hiring someone to find a missing person, or spend five dollars on a letter that might make them call you back? Hands up for the letter. Everybody? Good, then you already get this lesson. The Final Warning Letter is the last cheap step before the firm has to pick between two expensive ones: paying to find the client, or the attorney moving to end the case. So the letter has two jobs. It has to be specific enough that the client actually answers, and documented enough to back up whatever comes next. Now here's the teaser. There's one mistake that wastes the firm's money and weakens the whole record, and new Case Managers make it constantly. It has to do with three things being true at the same time. {name}, I'll reveal it on the next slide. Guess what the three things are.
why.ask: {name}, what's the risk of spending the firm's money on a search before the letter's deadline has even passed?

theory.say: Here's the reveal I promised. This letter is one last written notice before the firm searches for the client or the attorney moves to withdraw. It goes two ways at once. Certified mail proves it was delivered. Email is what people actually read. Each one covers the other's blind spot. Because certified mail has one secret talent: nobody is ever home to sign for it. That little green card comes back unclaimed more reliably than anything else in this business. Then the three-criteria gate. Think of it like a door with three locks: the ladder is done, the letter is sent, and the letter's deadline has passed. All three, not one. Only then do we skip-trace, which is just a paid search for someone's current address and phone number. Because it costs the firm money, the attorney has to approve it. And withdrawal, meaning the firm officially stops representing the client, is decided only by the attorney, under firm and court rules. {name}, which of those three locks do you think people forget to check?
theory.ask: {name}, which of these terms have you met before, and where would it show up on John Doe's file?

frame.say: Before I show you the next three steps, {name}, a prediction: of Steps 4, 5 and 6, how many do you think the Case Manager actually drives? Hold your number. Step 4 is the Final Warning Letter. It lists every earlier attempt, gives the client 7 to 14 days to respond, and warns that the firm may withdraw. It goes by certified mail and email. Step 5 is the decision point. If there's still no answer, the attorney decides whether to file a Notice or a Motion to Withdraw, which is the paperwork telling the court the firm is stepping off the case. Step 6 is closing the file, marked No response, withdrew per protocol, with every proof kept. And the reveal: you really drive just one, the letter. But you build the record that makes the other two possible. A sloppy letter makes Step 5 a gamble. A clean one makes it routine.
frame.ask: {name}, if John Doe went silent today, how far would his file be from Step 4?

rules.say: The rules. Step 4 goes by certified mail and email. Both, not either. The letter lists the earlier attempts, sets a deadline of 7 to 14 days and warns that withdrawal is possible. And confirm the address first. I once saw a perfect warning letter, beautifully written, mailed to the client's old apartment. The new tenant signed for it, read it, and called us asking if he could take over the case. True story, more or less. A letter to a stale address proves nothing. At Step 5, the attorney may file to withdraw. That's counsel's call. Skip-tracing starts only when all three locks are open and counsel approves it with the full log attached. The lazy letter says we've tried several times. The high-value letter says called 02/10, voicemail 02/13, and so on, with real dates. The letter can say withdrawal is possible. It can never judge the claim or announce the case is over.
rules.ask: {name}, why both certified mail and email, when either one would technically get the letter there?

model.say: Two panels here, and the most important thing on this slide is one tiny word. See if you can spot it. On the left is the letter on letterhead, with four orange badges marking what it must contain: the earlier attempts, listed; a response deadline of 7 to 14 days; notice that withdrawal is possible; and how to respond. Above it, certified mail and email joined by a bold AND. That's the tiny word, {name}. Not or. And. On the right is the Step 5 fork. It starts with one question: did a response come in by the deadline? If yes, the file picks right back up. If no, you hit a gate with three chips: ladder done, letter sent, deadline passed. Only then do you reach the skip-trace and the attorney's decision. It's drawn as a gate on purpose, because people love to sneak around it.
model.ask: {name}, what happens on this picture if only two of those three chips are true?

job.say: Here's how it runs on the job. Your Step 3 escalation is done and there's still nothing. So you draft the Final Warning Letter in the Action Plan Editor, the screen where we build letters and plans from the firm's templates, with every earlier attempt listed and the deadline and withdrawal notice in place. You confirm the current address and send it from CMS Documents, Outgoing, by certified mail and email, both logged, certified receipt kept. Then the deadline passes. And of course, the day after it passes, the client strolls back in with, hey, did you guys need something? Like he just went out for milk. That's fine, because the log still proves we did everything right. Now you check all three locks in the log, and only then do you escalate to Atty. Thorne through Tasks, asking for skip-trace approval and the Step 5 decision. Why care about all this paperwork? Because if this case ever goes sideways, a judge or a bar complaint looks at exactly this record. A clean letter protects the client's claim, the firm and you. {name}, which piece of this would you be most nervous about getting wrong?
job.ask: {name}, what's the first thing you'd check in the log before you escalate to Atty. Thorne?

dodont.say: 3 Clues, 1 Rule, round two. Three clues, revealed one at a time. The second you've got it, call Do or Don't and name the rule. {name}, you're up first, and the rest of you can steal if they miss. You'll see good habits, like listing attempts with real dates, because we have tried several times isn't evidence, and asking in-house help to confirm an address you can't verify. You'll see traps, like triggering a skip-trace when only one lock is open, or writing we are withdrawing in a letter the attorney never approved. That's the hard line. You build the record, the attorney decides to withdraw. On Day 5 we'll go deep on skip-tracing, process servers, the people who hand court papers to someone in person, and certified notice. Today's the trigger. Now your mystery for the drafting activity: Atty. Thorne wants a letter that's urgent but not threatening. {name}, find the one sentence in a typical draft that quietly turns urgent into a threat.
dodont.ask: {name}, who decides that representation is ending, and who tells the client?

case.say: Something just landed on the file, and before I reveal it, {name}, guess how many days a client can go quiet before it's a problem. Shout a number. Here it is, dated 02/16/2026, file LSH-2026-MVA-770412. Six days with no contact from John Doe. His last logged contact was 02/10/2026. He missed his check-in call on 02/13/2026. The phone system shows two calls to his mobile, both voicemail, and here's the twist: neither one is in the Communications Log, the file's diary of every contact. No treatment start recorded. His emergency contact is Margaret Doe, at (555) 010-2291, and Step 1 of the No Contact Protocol is due today. And check that number before you climb the ladder. I once called a client's number on file three times and got the same pizza place every time. By call three, they had my order memorized. Now, {name}, read the bad log entry out loud for us. Called client, no answer. Be honest, most of us have written that. Here's why it hurts: six months from now, nobody can tell when, which number, or what happened next. A note that vague is basically a sticky note in the rain.
case.ask: {name}, what's missing from called client, no answer that a supervisor would need six months from now?

task.say: Your turn to run the No Contact Protocol on John Doe's file. Start with Step 1, the internal review in the CMS Case Summary, and name the deadlines live right now. No dialling first. Then rebuild the attempts already made, those two missing voicemails, and carry the Step 2 ladder forward in the Communications Log: every attempt with date, time, channel and outcome, plus the next action and its due date. Then the fun part, a live call with Margaret Doe. {name}, you might be the one on the phone. Say who you are, confirm she's the emergency contact on file, ask her to have John call the firm by a set date, and confirm his best number and current address, all without sharing any case details. That last part trips people up, because Margaret will ask, is he okay, is the case okay? Your answer is friendly and gives her nothing about the case. Fair warning, emergency contacts aren't always thrilled to hear from us. I once had a mom pick up and say, he's thirty-four, why am I still his answering service? You hand in a full Step 1 review, an unbroken Step 2 log, and your call on Step 3.
task.ask: {name}, before you log anything, which deadline is running on this file right now?

check.say: Check your work against these, and let's draw the line between okay and excellent. The okay version says, I called, I emailed. The excellent version shows Step 1 done first, with status, live deadlines and last contact reviewed. Both earlier voicemails are logged with date, time and channel. The phone rung is cleared with at least two attempts, then email and text, not more calls. Margaret is used, the rung people forget most. Every entry has date, time, channel and outcome, and a next action with a due date. Your Step 3 impact names the SOL of 02/06/2028 and the treatment that hasn't started. And nothing threatens to drop the case. Here's why this matters down the road: that missing treatment start is the seed of the 14-Day Gap, a stretch with no doctor visits that an insurance company will use to cut the offer. So here's your mystery, {name}: if John's silent now, what does the adjuster say about it in six months, and how does your log answer them?
check.ask: {name}, if you called his mobile three times, how many channels have you actually used?

case.say: A note from Atty. Thorne just landed on the file, dated 02/21/2026. Before I read it, {name}, guess how many days it's been since we heard from John. Closer than you'd like? Here it is. Eleven days, no word, and no treatment we know of. The phone rung is cleared, emails and texts are out, Margaret Doe has been tried, and it's all logged. Atty. Thorne wants the Final Warning Letter drafted for review Monday morning: every attempt with its date, a response date, and how to reach us, by certified mail and email. Withdrawal is possible, not decided, and the letter says nothing about John's claim. Here's the hard part. It has to be urgent but not threatening. I've seen first drafts that read like a love letter, please call when you get a chance, no rush, and drafts that read like a ransom note. Neither one gets a call back.
case.ask: {name}, give me one sentence that would make this letter sound threatening rather than urgent?

task.say: You'll draft the Step 4 Final Warning Letter to John Doe in the Action Plan Editor, using the warning letter template. List every earlier attempt with its date. Set a response deadline inside the 7 to 14 day window, warn that withdrawal is possible, and tell him exactly how to respond. Every sentence stays inside the UPL line. UPL is the unauthorized practice of law, meaning giving legal advice when you're not a lawyer. So nothing about how strong his claim is, nothing about what silence does to it legally, and nothing saying the case is being dropped. Then write down what has to be true before a skip-trace can start, and whose approval Step 5 needs. {name}, you'll read your opening line to the room when you're done, so make it a good one. You hand in a ready-to-send letter with both deliveries logged and the escalation recorded.
task.ask: {name}, whose approval does the Step 5 decision need, and where will you record that?

check.say: Swap drafts with the person next to you and grade each other. Fun fact: a good warning letter is the fastest way to make a missing client reappear. Half the time they call within the hour asking why we're being so dramatic. First, {name}, read us the banned and compliant pairs out loud; it'll save someone a full rewrite. Now the difference between passable and excellent. The passable letter has a deadline of as soon as possible. The excellent one has a real date inside the 7 to 14 day window. Look for the firm's name and file reference, and the date of loss, 02/06/2026. Earlier attempts listed with dates. Withdrawal reads as possible, not decided. At least two ways to respond. Certified mail and email both recorded, address confirmed first. Nothing about claim value or legal consequence, so no you will lose your case. Skip-trace locks written down, Step 5 noted as Atty. Thorne's. Why it matters: this one letter can be the difference between a client who comes back to finish treatment and a case that closes for nothing. And your mystery: if John does call back, what's the very first thing you check on his file?
check.ask: {name}, does your partner's letter tell John what's needed and by when, without telling him what happens to his case?

questions.say: Welcome to the game show portion of the day. Your answers come from this file, in your own words, typed under each question, but I'm going to warm you up out loud first. {name}, lightning round: name the six steps of the No Contact Protocol in order. Go. Anyone can steal if they stall. On the test you'll set out all six steps with what's required at each. You'll state the protocol's three purposes and say which one protects the firm rather than the client. Here's a hint, because people answer this one shallowly: protection from liability, meaning the firm being able to show it did its job if someone complains later, is the purpose most people leave out. It's exactly why the record is built the way it is. Then the case of the lazy colleague, who logged three voicemails on three days and called the ladder done. Tell me what's wrong and what the log should show.
questions.ask: {name}, which of the three purposes do you think is easiest to forget?

summary.say: Now your Self-Summary, where you put the principles in your own words. Here's the scenario. It's 04/08/2026. Riverton Spine & Rehab reports John Doe has missed two visits, he isn't answering anyone, and Dana Whitfield has asked John for a Recorded Statement. Tell me what you do first, second and third, and what each step protects. This one pulls it all together: the running SOL, a Treatment Gap that's hardening, and the claims work that has to keep moving anyway. Keep in mind, too, that the gap you're watching build here is the same 14 days defense counsel will ask John Doe about at his deposition on Day 5.
summary.ask: {name}, of those three problems, which one protects the most if you deal with it first?

scale.say: Last step is your Skill Scale. Rate yourself honestly, one to five, on each competency, then submit it. One to five isn't a grade. It's a snapshot of where you are today. When I get these back, I'll compare your rating with your Knowledge Check score, and wherever there's a wide gap, either way, we'll have a short chat. Overrating and underrating both tell me something useful. Fair warning: last batch, someone rated themselves a five on everything and then put Margaret Doe down as the defendant. We still talk about it. Now, a mystery to take with you. John's transportation fell apart on 04/01, and his visits started slipping right after. {name}, before tomorrow, dig through the file and tell me what we could have done the day his ride ended, like asking Riverton about transportation help, and who we should have told that same day.
scale.ask: {name}, which competency here are you least sure how to rate, and why?

why.say: Game: what's the date? I give you a date, you tell me what's due. {name}, 04/07/2026. Anyone? Here's a hint: count six weeks from John Doe's first therapy visit on 02/24/2026. It was his week-6 mark of care, the day the doctors check whether therapy is actually working. And John Doe wasn't there. Here's why that matters. On an LOP, nobody denies the next six visits in real time. The insurance company, Keystone, does it later, at the demand, by calling the care unnecessary or the injury minor. That leaves you as the only real-time check that John Doe's plan is working, and the person who acts the very day it isn't. No pressure. And by the end of this lesson, you'll know exactly why he missed it. Here's a hint: it's not because he felt better.
why.ask: {name}, on an LOP file, who denies unnecessary care, and when, and what does that make you?

map.say: Here's the road for monitoring treatment, before we get into it. Five steps, and {name}, I'm going to test you on the middle three in about ninety seconds, so lock them in. You check in on visits, pain, function and any barrier, which is anything stopping him getting to care. When something's off, you name the variance, the type of problem: clinical, which is medical, psychosocial, which is life or mood, or systemic, which is the system being stuck. Then you run A-C-T. Assess, where medical danger goes to the provider and legal danger goes to Atty. Thorne. Coordinate, where you clarify with the office and remove the barrier. And Track, where every fix attempt goes into a GIRP note, a short note of the Goal, the Intervention, the Response and the Plan, facts only. Okay, {name}: A, C, T. Go.
map.ask: {name}, what are the three steps of A-C-T, and which one ends up written in the GIRP note?

theory.say: Knowing the Standard Treatment Map is what separates a Case Manager who watches a recovery from one who drives it, because care that drifts off the map is what triggers denials and IMEs, the exams the insurance company orders from its own doctor. Quick recap in plain words. Acute is days 1 to 14: the ER, imaging, first therapy and proving the crash caused the injury. Sub-acute runs weeks 2 to 8: active therapy, specialists and measured gains. Restorative is weeks 9 to 24: injections, work hardening, which is therapy that rebuilds the strength for his actual job, and anything blocking a return to work. Then maintenance: home exercise and visits as needed. Maximum Medical Improvement, or MMI, is the doctor saying more care won't make him better. It closes treatment and opens the pre-demand. When a client drifts off the map, you ask why first, before the funding stops. The watcher writes "missed visits." The driver writes why, and what's being done about it. {name}, be a driver for me.
theory.ask: {name}, which phase do you think John Doe was in when he missed his week-6 mark?

theory2.say: A few more ideas you'll lean on. The A-C-T protocol is your immediate action for any red flag: Assess the danger, Coordinate the fix and Track it, and that record is what gives Atty. Thorne his why. "Reasonable and necessary" is the insurer's test for paying: is the care normal for this kind of crash, and is there a measurable gain, not just "I hurt less"? SMART goals, meaning specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, like the week-6 measures, are what hold up with doctors and adjusters alike. And there's the stakeholder triad: the clinical loop, the legal loop and the money loop, with you as the switchboard in the middle. One broken loop can stall a case for months. {name}, here's a fun one. "John will feel better soon" is a wish, not a goal. Turn it into a SMART goal for me.
theory2.ask: {name}, what would a SMART goal for John Doe's next six weeks of therapy actually sound like?

frame.say: Here's the map phase by phase, with a test at the end, so {name}, keep your finger on John Doe's file. Acute is days 1 to 14: the ER, an MRI or CT, a brace, rest and ice, and first therapy, while we establish causation, meaning the crash caused it, and PIP coverage. Sub-acute is weeks 2 to 8, with active therapy two or three times a week and specialist follow-up. That's where the week-6 check lives, looking for 20 to 30 percent better range of motion. Restorative is weeks 9 to 24: work hardening, injections, emotional adjustment and finding the barriers to going back to work. Maintenance comes after week 24, with home exercise and visits as needed while we watch for the doctor's MMI finding. MMI is the finish line. Treatment closes, and the pre-demand audit opens. Here's why the map matters for money: an adjuster lays John's records over this exact map, and every spot where they don't line up is a spot where the offer drops.
frame.ask: {name}, on 04/08/2026, day 61 of John Doe's file, where on this map is he sitting?

rules.say: Now the rules. Monitor outcomes, not just attendance. Ask about visits, pain and what he can't do at work or home, and hunt the barriers, inside ones like fear or mood and outside ones like transport or money. On 04/08/2026, day 61, he's in week 9. His week-6 mark fell on 04/07/2026, which is 02/24/2026 plus 42 days, and the next step, whether that's medication, injections or a specialist, is the doctor's decision. Name the variance before you fix it. Run A-C-T for every red flag, and adjust the plan first, because it's usually the plan, not the client. Climb the ladder one documented rung at a time: clinical, then administrative, then legal. Write every intervention as a GIRP note. You coordinate care; you never direct it. Never tell him to skip treatment, or that missed visits cut his claim. And make friends with the clinic's front desk. The doctor runs the treatment, but the front desk runs the building, the schedule and possibly the weather. They'll know he missed before anyone.
rules.ask: {name}, why does writing "this will help the case" in a GIRP note put the file at risk?

model.say: This picture shows how A-C-T fits inside monitoring rather than beside it. There's a navy ring with the question "Is the plan working?" in the middle. Down at about four o'clock, a red detect node breaks out into three steps: assess, coordinate, track. Then notice the arrow from track. It curves right back up into the ring. Up in the corner is the treatment map, with a marker on restorative, week 9, 04/08/2026. And on the left are the three variance chips, clinical, psychosocial and systemic, with psychosocial lit up, because what derailed John wasn't the clinic or a payer, it was what the crash left him with. A-C-T isn't a detour from monitoring. It closes back into it.
model.ask: {name}, why is psychosocial the variance that's highlighted for John Doe, rather than clinical or systemic?

job.say: Let's walk through a few weeks of this file. A provider's missed-visit alert comes in. That same day, you reach for John Doe, and if he's gone silent you start the No Contact Protocol, logging the first attempt in the Communications Log the day the alert arrived. At week 6, 04/07/2026, you ask the provider for the re-evaluation measures: range of motion, pain score and disability index. Whether a PHQ-9 or GAD-7 screen is indicated is the provider's call, and anything putting his mental health in the record gets flagged to Atty. Thorne. If the barrier isn't fixed at the clinical rung, you climb one rung with a written notice to the carrier causing it, copied to Atty. Thorne, and only property facts to Keystone PD, with each rung dated. Red flags that can cost the claim go to Atty. Thorne with the fix you attempted.
job.ask: {name}, why does the GIRP note need to be dated the day the alert arrives, not the day you finish?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Three clues come up one at a time. When you've got it, call Do or Don't and name the rule. {name}, you're scorekeeper. You'll be watching for red flags to raise with the provider, like more than 12 sessions with no gain, therapy that's only passive, like heat packs and massage, or two or more missed visits. You'll see yellow flags reported with a plan, in the map's language. Then there's proofreading left and right, because everything on this file is right-sided, and one billing office typing "left" turns John into a medical miracle with a moving injury. And recording a problem the day it happens, so it never needs the reconstruction the 14-Day Gap does. The traps are keeping the plan unchanged through a crisis, blaming John, or jumping to Atty. Thorne before the clinical and administrative rungs. Now the mystery. John has missed two visits. What if, next, he stops picking up the phone too? {name}, what's the first thing you'd do, and how would you prove you did it?
dodont.ask: {name}, what argument from the defense does a factual A-C-T record answer later on?

why.say: Game time: guess the number. I've got John Doe's PIP Log up with the right-hand column covered. PIP, by the way, is coverage on the car he was riding in that pays Medical Bills no matter who caused the crash. Harbor Point has paid $685.00, $640.00, $2,395.00 and then $640.00 for the 03/27/2026 visit, out of $5,000. {name}, how much is left? Closest guess wins bragging rights. {name}, you're checking the math. It's $640.00. Why do I care if you can add? Because treatment is the engine room of this file, and somebody has to pay for every visit while the claim is open. On this file three payers stand in line: Harbor Point PIP, then Peach State, his Health Plan, then a Letter of Protection. Get the order wrong and a bill an earlier payer would have covered turns into a lien, a debt that comes straight out of John Doe's check at the end. And fair warning: medical billing departments speak a language nobody else on Earth speaks. By the end of today you'll be fluent. Almost.
why.ask: {name}, with $640.00 of PIP left, where does the rest of a bigger bill go next?

theory.say: Four ideas in plain words, and a riddle first. One of these payers can pay a bill today and then come back after the settlement asking for its money back. {name}, tell me which one when we're done. Once the claim's set up, the Case Plan runs on three pillars: clinical care, how he's functioning, and subrogation management, which is a fancy phrase for who gets paid back from the settlement. The Payer Order is the default line: MedPay or PIP first, health insurance second, an LOP last. Keeping that order keeps the liens down. PIP is coverage for Medical Bills regardless of fault, up to its limit. Health insurance pays covered care at its contract rate. And a Letter of Protection is the client's signed agreement that a provider gets paid from any recovery, which makes it a lien on his net, meaning his take-home. So, {name}, the riddle? It's the Health Plan. It can hold a reimbursement right against the recovery. Lovely people, Health Plans. They just like their money back.
theory.ask: {name}, which of these payers have you dealt with in your own life, and which one is first in line on John Doe's file?

theory2.say: The other half is about keeping care moving. The Standard Treatment Map is the usual route: emergency, imaging, chiropractic and therapy, orthopedics, pain management, sometimes surgery, and every stop needs a payer. Monitoring progress means checking real results, not ticking boxes. The lazy check-in is "Hey John, how are you?" He says "Fine," and you've learned nothing. The high-value check-in is "How many visits did you make this week, what can you do now that you couldn't last month, and what might get in your way next week?" Crisis intervention is stepping in when care gets denied or stuck in paperwork, and fixing the immediate problem first. Pro tip: the fastest way to unstick a clinic is the one person in its billing office who actually answers the phone. They know which bill is stuck, why, and whose desk it's sitting on. And watch for medication red flags, like an opioid, a muscle relaxant and a sedative together, or doses climbing with no new diagnosis. You don't judge that yourself. You raise it with the provider. {name}, you're up.
theory2.ask: {name}, instead of asking John Doe how he is, what's one question you'd ask him about his plan?

frame.say: Here's the Payer Order, step by step, with a pop quiz hidden inside. {name}, one of these payers also covers lost wages. Shout it when you hear it. First you identify the payers: every source and its default order, and remember that who's actually primary is Atty. Thorne's call, not ours. Next is MedPay or PIP. Both pay regardless of fault, up to the limit. And there's your answer: PIP also pays 80% of lost income, where MedPay pays Medical Bills only. Then comes the Health Plan, which pays covered care at its contract rate but may claim money back from the recovery. The Letter of Protection is the last rung, for care the earlier payers can't carry, paid from any recovery on Atty. Thorne's terms. Think of the ladder like this: every rung you skip on the way up is a rung John Doe pays for on the way out. {name}, climb it for me.
frame.ask: {name}, where is John Doe on this ladder for his Riverton Spine & Rehab physical therapy, and why?

rules.say: Now the rules. In treatment, the question is always "Is the plan working?" Run the Payer Order: Harbor Point PIP, then Peach State, then an LOP. John claims the $5,000 PIP as a passenger in Kevin Alvarez's 2020 Ford Escape, because no policy in his household carries PIP. PIP pays in date order, never wages. When Crescent Pain & Spine billed Peach State on 05/15/2026 with $640.00 of PIP left, you tracked both ledgers and never re-routed a paid claim. Riverton Spine & Rehab got an LOP because it's out of network. Summit Imaging's 03/11/2026 MRI went to PIP. The lazy move is saying yes to every LOP request because it makes the provider go away. The high-value move is proving, from the ledger, which payer should cover it. LOP terms are Atty. Thorne's: you prepare, route, send once he approves, and confirm receipt. I once had a billing manager call me four times in one morning about an invoice dated that same morning. She wanted it paid yesterday. Smile, log it, and never promise a provider an amount, a reduction or a date.
rules.ask: {name}, Riverton and Summit Imaging both asked for an LOP. Why did only one of them get it?

model.say: This slide has an argument hidden in it, and I want you to find it before I say it. Here's the PIP Log, Harbor Point's $5,000, with five rows paid in date order. Above it there's a gauge draining in five steps, and the last one lands on $0.00 at 06/12/2026, in red. On the left is the payer rail: PIP first, Peach State second, and the LOP third, stamped counsel-approved terms. Along the bottom are two provider chips. Riverton Spine & Rehab has a tick for its LOP. Summit Imaging has a cross, because its bill went to PIP instead. {name}, what's the argument? Here it is: an LOP is the last rung of the Payer Order, not the first answer to a provider who asks. And here's why it matters for the settlement. Every LOP dollar is one somebody has to negotiate down later, or it comes out of John Doe's pocket. An LOP feels free on the day it's signed. It never feels free on the day the check arrives.
model.ask: {name}, what would a $2,395.00 LOP for Summit Imaging have cost John Doe at the end?

job.say: Picture a normal month on this file. A provider asks for an LOP. You run the Payer Order and prepare one on counsel's template only for care PIP and Peach State can't carry, then route it for approval from CMS Documents, Outgoing. The payer check is recorded first, and nothing goes out without Atty. Thorne. When PIP pays a bill, you post the payment, the running total and the balance on the PIP Log, and it ties to Harbor Point, hitting $5,000.00 on the 06/12/2026 visit. When an LOP statement arrives, you check every line against the visits, so through 04/02/2026 that's 16 visits at $185.00, or $2,960.00, all attended. For a new referral, you do a warm handoff, meaning John and the new office are on the same call, and you confirm the payer before the first visit. Why so fussy? Because at the demand the adjuster adds up our bills, and at the end the lien holders add them up too. If our numbers are the only clean numbers in the room, we win the argument. {name}, you're on the audit.
job.ask: {name}, if Riverton bills a date John Doe didn't attend, what do you do with that line?

dodont.say: Time for 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues in turn. Call Do or Don't as soon as you've got it, and name the rule. {name}, you're scorekeeper. Good habits include asking "Is the plan working?" at every contact, ending each call by asking what might get in the way of treatment this week, fixing conflicting provider notes straight away, and telling John which payer handles which bill, because cost worry left unanswered is how a client stops going. The traps are issuing an LOP just because a provider asked, telling a provider they'll be paid in full at settlement, mission creep, which means doing jobs that aren't yours, and handing Atty. Thorne raw records with no summary. Now the mystery. In a few months, a statement is going to land asking John Doe to pay $1,540.00 on a bill his Health Plan already processed. {name}, before the next lesson, think about it: does he owe it? The answer is hiding on a piece of paper that literally says THIS IS NOT A BILL.
dodont.ask: {name}, why is an LOP never really free for John Doe, even when the provider is happy with it?

why.say: Show of hands: who's ever opened a letter from their health insurance, read the whole thing, and still had no idea whether they owed money? Keep it up if you just paid it to make it go away. Yeah. That letter is called an EOB, an Explanation of Benefits, and it might be the most confusing document in America. It's not a bill. It's the Health Plan's report on what it did with a bill. Today you become the person who can read one. Take out RS26, Peach State's EOB. {name}, find the bottom line: what does John Doe owe Crescent for the injection? The EOB says $0.00. Every payer reports back. Peach State does it with an EOB, and Harbor Point does it with its PIP payment history. Read line by line, they tell you what was billed, what was paid, what was written off and what John Doe may still owe. Those papers are the proof behind every medical number in the demand and every lien we negotiate. Get them right, and nobody slips a wrong number past us.
why.ask: {name}, reading RS26, what does John Doe actually owe Crescent Pain & Spine for the injection, and which line tells you?

theory.say: Four terms, and one of them sounds like a robot from a space movie. Every payer reports back on a bill: the Health Plan with an EOB, and PIP with its payment history, and you read both before you ever touch a lien. An EOB is the plan's account of one processed claim. Not a bill, just proof of who paid what. Billed versus allowed is the first thing to see. Billed is what the provider charged. Allowed is what the plan agreed to pay under its contract. In network, the gap gets written off, which means it simply disappears. Remark codes are the little codes that explain each line, and here's our robot: CO-45 is the write-off code. AC1 flags a possible accident. And member responsibility, meaning the deductible, copay and coinsurance, is the most an in-network provider may bill the patient. The lazy reader looks at the total and moves on. The high-value reader reads every line, because every line is a number someone may try to put in front of John Doe later. {name}, quick one.
theory.ask: {name}, which of these terms have you seen on your own Medical Bills, and what did it mean there?

theory2.say: Four more ideas, and these are where money quietly gets lost. Balance billing is when a provider bills the patient for the part the plan already wrote off. In network that isn't allowed, so it's an error, not a lien and not a debt. The PIP payment history is the carrier's list of every check: the date of service, the amount paid and the limit remaining. Exhaustion is what happens once that limit's spent. Later bills come back unpaid, and you send them to the next payer. And reconciliation means matching every provider balance to each payer's EOB or check, so no bill that's already been paid ever becomes a lien against John Doe. Here's a real one. A client once paid a balance bill because, and I quote, "it had a barcode, so it looked official." The barcode was very official. The bill was wrong. It took us two months to get his money back. {name}, help me out.
theory2.ask: {name}, if a provider bills John Doe for a write-off, is that a lien, a debt or an error?

frame.say: Here's how you read an EOB, top to bottom, every single time. {name}, one of these steps is the one people skip, and it's the one that costs the client. Guess which as I go. First, match the claim: the member ID, claim number, provider and date of service against the CMS treatment record. Then go from billed to allowed: the charge, what the plan allowed, and the amount it wrote off. Next is the patient's share, the deductible, copay and coinsurance, because member responsibility is the most a provider may bill. After that, what the plan paid, with its date and its check or electronic payment number, since that's where any payback claim starts. Read the remark codes: CO-45 explains the write-off, and AC1 flags an accident and the plan's right to be paid back. Finally, reconcile and log it against the provider's statement and the lien register, and flag any balance billing. The step people skip? That last one. They read it, nod, and never compare it to the provider's statement. That's how a $0.00 turns into a collections call.
frame.ask: {name}, which step would you be most tempted to skip on a busy Friday, and why?

rules.say: Here's the real one on John Doe's file. Peach State's EOB of 06/03/2026, claim PS-2605-449021, covers Crescent's 05/15/2026 epidural injection, a shot of medicine near the spine for pain, and it says THIS IS NOT A BILL. Crescent billed $3,400.00 and the plan allowed $1,860.00. The $1,540.00 difference is Crescent's write-off. The plan paid $1,860.00, and member responsibility is $0.00. CO-45 explains that write-off, and AC1 is how Peach State's right to be paid back attaches. Now Crescent's 07/01/2026 statement asks John Doe for $1,540.00. That's a balance bill, not a debt and not a lien. The lazy Case Manager forwards it to John with "FYI." The high-value one documents it, routes it to Atty. Thorne that day, drafts a correction request and tells John what's happening. Peach State's claim starts at $1,860.00, never $3,400.00, and its accident questionnaire goes to Atty. Thorne. Harbor Point's five checks total $5,000.00, exhausted 06/26/2026. You read and reconcile; whether he owes anything is counsel's call.
rules.ask: {name}, Crescent's $1,540.00 statement: is it a lien we missed, or a bill nobody owes, and which EOB line proves it?

model.say: Two documents, side by side, and a little detective work. On the left is Peach State's EOB for claim PS-2605-449021, with that red stamp, THIS IS NOT A BILL. Six rows: billed $3,400.00, allowed $1,860.00, the $1,540.00 adjustment, $0.00 deductible, $1,860.00 paid, and $0.00 member responsibility. Each orange tag tells you where that number goes on the file. On the right is Harbor Point's payment history, five checks with a limit bar falling from $5,000.00 to nothing, stamped exhausted 06/26/2026. And underneath sits Crescent's 07/01/2026 statement for $1,540.00, with a dashed line back to that $0.00 row and a question: balance bill? {name}, that dashed line is the whole case. Billing departments don't usually do this on purpose. Somebody in an office somewhere pressed "send statements" on every account with a balance, and nobody looked at the EOB. You're the one who looks.
model.ask: {name}, which row on Peach State's EOB is the most Crescent may bill John Doe?

job.say: Let's run it as it happens on the file. An EOB arrives, and you post billed, allowed, adjustment, paid and member share against the visit in CMS Liens and Documents, so the $1,860.00 plan payment is logged and claim PS-2605-449021 is linked to the visit. A PIP check clears, and you post it on the PIP Log with the date of service and the limit remaining, until it ties to Harbor Point's history with $0.00 left after 06/26/2026. Then a patient statement shows a balance. You compare it with the EOB's member responsibility, flag the $1,540.00, tell Atty. Thorne the same day and draft the correction request. When Peach State's itemized lien arrives, you match each line to an EOB and to the collision, so only those lines stand. Here's the payoff. At settlement, Peach State will want its money back. If you've matched every line, we pay back what's really owed. If you haven't, they'll happily take more, and it comes straight out of John's check. {name}, think like a lien auditor for a second.
job.ask: {name}, what would you do with a line on Peach State's lien that no EOB supports?

dodont.say: 3 Clues, 1 Rule, EOB edition. Three clues, one at a time. Call Do or Don't and name the rule. {name}, you're on the first buzz, and {name}, you're keeping score. The good habits are reading every EOB down to member responsibility before you answer a balance question, asking each provider for an itemized statement showing every payer's credit, keeping billed and paid on the same CMS line, and telling John what you're doing and when he'll hear back. The traps are logging a lien at the billed amount instead of what the plan paid, treating a write-off as something he owes, and sending a bill to PIP after it ran out on 06/26/2026. One number to hold onto: Peach State can claim back $1,860.00, never $3,400.00. Now the mystery for the next lesson. John Doe's PIP was supposed to cover some lost wages too, $1,267.20 of them. He never got a cent. Nobody stole it, and nobody forgot to file it. {name}, figure out where it went.
dodont.ask: {name}, after Harbor Point's $0.00 line on 06/26/2026, where does John Doe's next bill go?

why.say: Game time: Prove It. The adjuster says the gap proves John Doe healed. You've got thirty seconds to shout out everything you'd collect to prove he didn't. Go. {name}, you're writing them up. Good list. Now let's sort it into two boxes: things written down at the time, and things written up for the claim. Here's the reveal on last block's mystery. The paper made before anyone thought about a claim is the 02/07/2026 Riverton Drug receipt, one day after the crash, for pain relief. Nobody wrote that for a lawsuit. Records made at the time do the heavy lifting: provider notes that place the pain at the collision, histories that agree, the EMS report and the work records, and later a causation opinion, which is a doctor's letter linking the injury to the crash. Anything in the other box, a record made to order, destroys the very case it was meant to save.
why.ask: {name}, which item on our list would an adjuster find hardest to argue with, and why?

theory.say: Here's the why behind the paperwork: continuity is proved by what the record already shows, never by what it's asked to say. Continuity of care just means an unbroken path of treatment, each step following from the last, and that chain is exactly what an adjuster tests. A Treatment Gap is any break in it, and adjusters read a gap as minor, healed or unrelated. Records made at the time, written by EMS, doctors and employers as things happened, are your strongest proof, because nobody wrote them for the claim. And consistent histories, the same story of how, when and where it hurts across every chart, make continuity believable. On TV, the detective finds one magic clue. In real life, you find twelve boring receipts that agree with each other. Boring wins. {name}, before I ask, take a guess at who wrote the first thing about John Doe's neck.
theory.ask: {name}, who on John Doe's file wrote something down about his neck before anyone thought about a claim?

theory2.say: Four more ideas, and one of them can end a career. A causation opinion is a treating doctor's opinion linking the injury to the collision. It's the bridge across a gap, and Atty. Thorne requests it, not us. Record integrity means a record changes only by its author's own dated addendum, an added note with a date on it. Altering a record can be evidence tampering or fraud. That's the career-ender. Excuse notes prove only what their author saw or ordered at a visit, so days nobody examined him need other proof. And generic notes, ones that don't tie the complaints to the collision, weaken causation. Under A-C-T, those get flagged to Atty. Thorne. You don't fix them yourself. The lazy fix is calling the clinic and asking them to “update” a note. The high-value move is flagging it and letting counsel decide. {name}, think about the week of 02/09.
theory2.ask: {name}, what proves John Doe couldn't work 02/09 through 02/13, when no doctor saw him?

frame.say: These are the treatment red flags, and each one is a gift to the defense. Before I go through them, {name}, guess which one shows up most. Hold it. In physical therapy, more than 12 sessions with no gain and no specialist or imaging suggested reads as a stalled plan or over-treatment. Passive care only, meaning heat packs, TENS, which is a little electrical pulse machine, and massage with no exercise, is feel-good care adjusters discount. Two or more missed appointments let the defense say the injury wasn't serious. Surgery recommended before therapy or injections, outside an emergency, invites a challenge on whether it was reasonable and necessary. In pain management, an opioid, a muscle relaxant and a sedative together, with doses rising, is a safety risk. And in the records, left and right switched, or notes about life stress instead of the crash, weaken both credibility and causation. The answer to my guess? Missed appointments, by a mile.
frame.ask: {name}, which of these red flags do you see on John Doe's file right now?

rules.say: Here are the rules. Continuity is proved by records made at the time, then by a doctor's opinion that reads them, and never by explanations made to order. Read every history for three things: how it happened, the collision; when it started, 02/06/2026; and where it hurts, the neck and right arm, since the 2021 visits were low back. If the therapy notes and Dr. Reyes disagree, flag it to Atty. Thorne that day. Never ask a provider to change, back-date or add to a record, and never order an excuse note. For 02/09 to 02/13, Northgate's Attendance Record is the proof. The EMS report covers day zero, so record “declined transport” exactly as written. Keep the 02/07/2026 Riverton Drug receipt and the full text thread to Margaret Doe. A causation opinion is Atty. Thorne's request; you assemble and track, never draft. And no, “I was going to scan it, I was just busy” doesn't count. If it's not in the file, it doesn't exist.
rules.ask: {name}, Riverton's front desk offers to add a line saying the pain began at the crash. What do you say, and who do you tell?

model.say: This is a compare board, and the heading says it all: made at the time versus made to order. {name}, read me the dates on the left card while I count them. On the left, under a green rule, is what counts: the 02/06 EMS report, the 02/07 receipt, the 02/09 to 02/13 call-outs, the 02/20 urgent care note and the 06/19 Causation Letter. On the right, in red, is what never happens, every item struck through. Now look along the bottom. There's a timeline from 02/06 to 06/19 with the left card's documents pinned onto it, so you can see the proof was being laid down while the gap was actually happening. Timing is what makes a document believable. And that's real money: a gap the adjuster can't explain away is a gap he can't use to cut the offer.
model.ask: {name}, why does the 06/19 Causation Letter belong in the left column, even though it came months later?

job.say: Here's the rhythm on the job. A provider record arrives, and you compare how, when and where against the other histories on the treatment timeline. Either it's logged consistent, or it's flagged with the conflicting line quoted. If one history conflicts with another, you flag it to Atty. Thorne through Tasks that same day, and you don't call the provider about the wording. When Atty. Thorne decides to seek a causation opinion, you assemble the records for his letter and put the follow-up on the calendar. And when a work or excuse note arrives, you check the signer, the date and the covered days against the visit record. I once watched a Case Manager print the entire file, four hundred pages, “just in case,” to find one date. The date was on page two of the CMS timeline. Search first, print never. {name}, you'd have found it in ten seconds, right?
job.ask: {name}, why shouldn't you call the provider yourself to sort out a conflicting history?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. One clue at a time; the moment you know, call Do or Don't and name the rule. {name}, you're on the first buzz. The good habits: collecting what already exists before asking for anything new, quoting records exactly, flagging conflicting statements rather than fixing them, and keeping every interruption visible on the timeline with its dates. The traps: asking a provider to “clarify” a note in a way that tells them what to write, and leaving the gap off the timeline and hoping nobody notices. And here's the twist. A stronger note isn't always better. A note that shows up after the firm asked for it, saying exactly what the firm needed, is the weakest document in the file. Now your mystery: every number in John Doe's case is about to get added up for the demand. Somewhere in those bills, one charge appears that shouldn't. {name}, you'll hunt for it next.
dodont.ask: {name}, why would your fingerprints on Dr. Reyes's wording make her letter worthless?

why.say: Quick game: guilty or not proven. I'll say a fact, you tell me if it proves Keystone has to pay for John's neck. Robert Smith was cited for failure to stop. {name}? Ruth Calloway, the witness, saw it happen. {name}? Here's the twist: neither one is enough. Proving negligence, that Smith was careless, is only half the battle in personal injury law. The other half is causation and damages: proving that this collision, and nothing else, caused his C5-C6 herniation, which is a disc bulging out between two neck bones, his Medical Bills and the right-arm symptoms he still has. Keystone already has two other causes lined up, the 14-day gap and his 2021 chiropractic visits. The document that links the crash to the injury is the Causation Letter, and on this file it's Dr. Alana Reyes's letter of 06/19/2026. The demand, the rebuttal and every binder after it lean on that letter. Think of it like a group project: Smith did the crash, but somebody still has to prove who did the damage.
why.ask: {name}, if Keystone admitted fault tomorrow, what could it still refuse to pay for?

doc.say: Before you ever handle one, let's open this document up, and I'll give you the punchline last. A Causation Letter is a formal opinion from a medical professional, a treating physician, a surgeon or an independent medical expert, linking the accident to the specific injuries. Its legal purpose is the half negligence can't prove: that the defendant's conduct directly caused the harm, the medical expenses and the ongoing limitations claimed. Its evidentiary role on our file, meaning the job it does as proof, is big. Dr. Reyes holds her opinions more likely than not, ties the herniation to 02/06/2026, and answers both the gap and the 2021 visits. {name}, guess what your job with this letter is. Here's the punchline: your handling is the letter's path, never its words. Atty. Thorne requests it, you assemble the records and docket the follow-up, you check it against the file when it lands, and you file it and cite it. The lazy Case Manager files it unread. The high-value one reads it the same day, because a wrong date in a doctor's letter is a gift to the defense. A Causation Letter that says "maybe" is a fortune cookie, not evidence.
doc.ask: {name}, which part of handling this letter belongs to you, and which part never does?

theory.say: Four ideas sit under this lesson, in plain words. First, the two halves. Duty and breach, meaning Smith had to drive safely and didn't, prove negligence. Causation and damages prove what it cost, and a claim needs both. Second, who writes it: a treating physician or surgeon who examined the patient, or an independent medical expert who reviews the records. Dr. Reyes is John Doe's treating spine surgeon. Third, reasonable medical probability, which simply means more likely than not. Words like possibly or could be generally fall short, and the exact standard is Atty. Thorne's to confirm. A doctor writing "possibly" is a Magic 8-Ball answer: ask again later. Fourth, prior conditions. A prior injury in the same body region turns the question into aggravation, whether the crash made an old problem worse. John Doe's 2021 care was for his low back, a different region, and Dr. Reyes says it's unrelated. {name}, which of those four would you bet the defense attacks first?
theory.ask: {name}, why does it matter that the 2021 visits were for his low back and not his neck?

rules.say: Here are the rules that keep this letter worth something. Atty. Thorne requests it, in his own letter, with John Doe's written authorization. You build the record set Dr. Reyes needs, and that means everything: the EMS report, the urgent-care note, Riverton Spine & Rehab's notes, the MRI report, Crescent's procedure note, and the 2021 Birch Avenue records too. Then you docket the follow-up and track the reply. The day it arrives, you check it against the file: date of loss 02/06/2026, C5-C6 on the right, the visit dates, the records she lists. A mismatch goes to Atty. Thorne. You file it under Medical, dated 06/19/2026, and cite it on the Gap Explanation Record. And you never draft, edit or suggest a word of it. {name}, here's the lazy move: leave out the 2021 records so the doctor never sees them. The high-value move: send them, because a doctor who never saw the prior records gets taken apart at deposition, and her whole opinion goes down with her. Hiding records from your own expert is like hiding the map from your own driver.
rules.ask: {name}, why send Dr. Reyes the 2021 records when they're the defense's argument?

model.say: This table turns Dr. Reyes's letter into a map of the fight. Before I read it, {name}, guess how many separate opinions she gives. Four. Her four opinions are on the left, the defense each one answers is in the middle, and the records holding it up are on the right. The delay is clinically consistent, which answers "he waited two weeks," with the EMS report and the 02/20 urgent-care note behind it. The herniation was more likely than not caused by the collision, which answers "degenerative," meaning just wear and tear from age, backed by the MRI's no significant degenerative change at the adjacent levels. The 2021 care is unrelated, which answers a pre-existing condition. And the treatment was reasonable and necessary, with future injections anticipated in the 06/12 MMI note, MMI meaning he's as good as he's going to get. Every opinion rests on a record, and that's why the record set matters so much. Pull one record out and the opinion on top of it wobbles like a table with a short leg.
model.ask: {name}, which opinion would be weakest if one record were missing from her set?

job.say: On the job it runs in four beats. When Atty. Thorne decides to request a causation opinion, you assemble the record set, prior records included, for his letter, and put the follow-up on the calendar. When the letter arrives on 06/19/2026, you check the date of loss, the injury level and side, the visit dates and the records listed against the file, and you log each one as matching, or quote the mismatch and flag it. Once it's checked, you file it and cite it on the Gap Explanation Record's 14-day band and in the audit's risks. And when the Demand Package comes together, the letter goes in beside the MRI report and the EMS report, served on 07/20/2026. Why does this matter? Because the adjuster reads the Causation Letter first and the bills second. I once saw a Causation Letter that described the wrong arm. The doctor fixed it in a day, but only because the Case Manager caught it before it went out. {name}, that's the job: be the person who catches it.
job.ask: {name}, what would you do if the letter listed the wrong date of loss?

dodont.say: Time for 3 Clues, 1 Rule. One clue at a time, and as soon as you know, call Do or Don't and name the rule. {name}, you're keeping score. {name}, you get first buzz. The good habits here are treating causation as half the case, sending the doctor the complete record set with the prior records in it, and reading the letter against the file the day it arrives. The traps are the ones that feel helpful. Suggesting the doctor's wording, or asking her to make it stronger. Leaving the 2021 records out so she never has to deal with them. And telling John Doe the letter means his case is worth more. Each of those either weakens the letter or crosses the UPL line, the line between sharing facts and giving legal advice. Now your mystery for the next lesson: Dr. Reyes's letter mentions an MMI note and future injections. When we total John Doe's Specials next, does a future injection count, and who decides?
dodont.ask: {name}, which of those traps would feel most tempting on a busy day, and why?

case.say: Two dates, two emails, and one of these providers is about to get a no. Guess which by the end. First date: 02/23/2026. This email just came in from Tammy Greer, Office Manager at Riverton Spine & Rehab. John Doe is booked for his chiropractic and therapy evaluation tomorrow, 02/24, they're out of network with Peach State, and they want a signed Letter of Protection and his HIPAA authorization, the form that lets them share his records, today. His first treatment was Riverton Urgent Care on 02/20/2026, $685.00, paid by Harbor Point PIP. Atty. Thorne has approved the LOP template, and John had three chiropractic visits in 2021 for low-back stiffness. Remember that 2021 detail. It's going to matter. Second date: 03/11/2026. Summit Imaging Center, booked for the neck MRI Dr. Reyes ordered on 03/05/2026, asks for an LOP too. Notice the word "today" in Tammy's email. Every provider's office wants it today. The really keen ones send the email at six in the morning, just to be sure. {name}, you take Riverton. {name}, you've got Summit.
case.ask: {name}, before you open the template, why does Riverton get an LOP?

task.say: Work both dates, and start each by running the Payer Order. On 02/23/2026 you prepare Riverton's LOP on the approved template, route it to Atty. Thorne for signature, and transmit it with the HIPAA authorization. Then you take the live call with Tammy Greer, the office manager: introduce John's case, confirm the clinic accepts the LOP, secure tomorrow's evaluation, and answer her questions on insurance, visit cadence and billing with facts. On 03/11/2026 you decline Summit's request in writing, naming Harbor Point PIP and proving it from the PIP Log. No payment is promised to either provider.
task.ask: {name}, summit says it won't do the MRI without an LOP. What do you say, and who do you tell?

check.say: Check your work before you log it. Was the LOP signed by John Doe and Atty. Thorne on 02/23/2026, before the 02/24 visit, with nothing signed by you? Does your baseline show the 2021 visits were low back, resolved, a different region? Is the rental's 03/19/2026 end calendared as a treatment risk? Summit's decline names PIP, proved from the ledger with $3,675.00 left, enough for the $2,395.00 MRI. And your call with Tammy Greer is written up, tasked and filed, with nothing promised. If she asked whether the firm guarantees full payment, the only right answer is the LOP's own terms and a referral to Atty. Thorne. "Don't worry, you'll be paid in full" fails, however friendly.
check.ask: {name}, when a provider asks whether they'll be paid in full, how do you answer them?

case.say: Something landed on the file on 03/04/2026, and before I open it, {name}, guess: good news or trouble? Let's see. The first records are in. Riverton Urgent Care's 02/20/2026 note says onset at the MVA, the motor vehicle accident, on 02/06/2026, getting worse, with numbness to the right hand since 02/18. The EMS Run Report records neck stiffness on 02/06/2026. John Doe's been at Riverton Spine & Rehab since 02/24/2026, and Margaret's rental runs to 03/19/2026. Now the trouble: nobody has asked him why he waited 14 days. Atty. Thorne wants him on a recorded call today: open questions, nothing suggested, no opinions on what it means, and a GIRP note when you're done. Two ways to fail before anyone dials: a leading question or a suggested reason, and any version of “won't matter” or “will hurt the case.” Hidden in this call are four separate reasons. Most people find two.
case.ask: {name}, knowing what's on this file, what question will you be most tempted to ask him first?

task.say: You'll run a recorded call with AI John Doe in the Call Simulator to find out why he first treated on 02/20/2026, fourteen days after the collision. Open on the record with the date, who's on the call, your role, his consent to recording, and that he can talk privately. Ask open questions, follow his words, and save yes-or-no questions for pinning dates and documents. There are four reasons to draw out. Find out who he told and what he kept, like the texts, the call-outs and the 02/07 receipt, then read his account back. Close by confirming his 03/05 consult and his transport after 03/19. Then hand in a privileged GIRP note in Case Notes, that's Goal, Intervention, Response, Plan, and a dated task for every document. {name}, you're calling first. {name}, you're listening and counting leading questions. And if he says “I was busy,” remember what we said: that's a chapter title, not an answer.
task.ask: {name}, which reason was hardest to get, and what question finally got it?

model.say: This is your run sheet for the call. The simulator screen on the left shows AI John Doe, recorded call, 03/04/2026, with the red recording dot and a transcript below. Under the transcript there's a meter counting your questions: open, closed and leading, and leading is in red. You want that one at zero. This isn't a TV interrogation room; nobody gets points for the dramatic “Admit it, you had no car!” On the right are four empty reason slots, each with a space for a document beside it, and they only fill in as you actually surface them. Underneath sits a red warning: a suggested reason earns a yes, not a fact. Reasons are earned by questions. You never supply them. The lazy call fills one slot and calls it done. The high-value call fills all four, each with its paper. {name}, what's your plan for the first two minutes?
model.ask: {name}, what happens to the three hidden reasons if you ask “Was it the car?” two minutes in?

check.say: Check the call and the note before you log, and I'm going to pick on a few of you. {name}, did the recording start with 03/04/2026, everyone on the call, your role, his spoken consent and privacy confirmed? Was your first question open, covering 02/06 to 02/20, with zero leading questions? Here's the full reveal, all four reasons in his words: no transport, with the Civic towed, Kevin Alvarez's Escape in the shop and no rental until 02/18/2026; thinking it was soreness, treated with ibuprofen and lidocaine patches; doubting his Peach State coverage and not knowing PIP, the coverage that pays his Medical Bills no matter who caused the crash, even existed; and the numbness from 02/18, working two shifts, then urgent care on his first day off. Did you surface the texts, the Northgate call-outs and the receipt? And grade your GIRP note as hard as the call: his words in quotation marks, a dated plan, labelled privileged. Your mystery: there's a second interruption later in his care. {name}, find the dates.
check.ask: {name}, does your GIRP note record an intervention and a plan, or only how John Doe felt?

case.say: The clock starts at 04/08/2026, with this alert from Riverton Spine & Rehab on LOP account RSR-26-0412. John Doe missed 04/03 and 04/07 with no call, his last visit was 04/02/2026, and he isn't answering the clinic's calls or texts. Your own last contact with him was a check-in on 03/31. As you work, the file keeps moving: he misses 04/09 and 04/14, his mother Margaret tells you on 04/10 that he's safe but keeping to himself, and on 04/16 the CMS fires its 14-day no-visit trigger. I'll release each update when you've earned it, including the call that comes in on 04/17.
