task.say: Here's the job. Start with the Step 1 review, then send your notices by escalating channel and log each one: a call and a text on 04/08, a call and an email on 04/09, then Margaret on 04/10. Escalate to Atty. Thorne and send the 10-day Final Warning Letter by certified mail and email, with a response date of 04/20/2026, and set the Drop Warning status. When John calls on 04/17, you run a trauma-informed interview: safety first, his pace, his choices, his words. You don't diagnose, you don't send him to a counselor, and you say nothing about his claim. With his consent you set up a call with Dr. Reyes and evening visits under the LOP, then you restore the file and confirm 04/21 and 04/23.
task.ask: {name}, why does the letter's 04/20 date not mean the file closes on 04/20?

If he ever mentions harming himself, he gets the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline and Atty. Thorne hears about it at once. Second, his choice and his pace. I ask before recording, I ask before going back to the crash, and I let the silences run. Third, his words, not my labels. Every time I get in a car my chest goes tight, I write it down exactly like that. What it is belongs to Dr. Reyes, and what it means for the claim belongs to Atty. Thorne.
model.ask: {name}, what's wrong with saying, kindly, that sounds like PTSD?

Did your notices climb by channel, 04/08, 04/09 and Margaret on 04/10, each with its date, time, channel and outcome? Did the Final Warning Letter go by certified mail and email, with 04/20/2026 as the response date, withdrawal possible and not decided, and nothing about the claim? In the interview, did you quote John's own words about the panic at the corner on 04/02, his sleep and his mood, and keep every label out of it? Then the restoration on 04/20: Drop Warning cleared, the 14-day trigger reset, the Action Plan updated. Four missed visits, 19 days, attendance on 04/21 and 04/23.

He just wants it somewhere he can actually get to. {name}, how close was your guess?
case.ask: {name}, before you call him back, which document on the file would you open first, and why?

After that, every task that follows is yours to do or to delegate, with an owner and a due date: the cancellation, the calendar, Parties, Peach State and the Lien Tracker, the records request, transport, the GIRP note, the report to Atty. Thorne, and the attendance check after 05/15/2026. The bare minimum is "I told John to call Lakeside." The high-value version is John booked, on the phone, before you hang up. {name}, you're making the call. {name}, you're playing Janelle.

No row says "someone should." Calling John back, reading Dr. Reyes's referral, verifying Crescent with Peach State, booking 05/15/2026 with John on the line, the calendar, the Parties entry, the Peach State billing and the Lien Tracker flag, transport, the GIRP note and the report are all done on 04/22/2026. Everyone had followed up. Nobody had done anything. {name}, spot the difference here.

check.say: Check your work before you log it. {name}, did you return the call on 04/22/2026 and record John's reasons in his own words? Did you verify Crescent's network status with Peach State, instead of repeating what he heard at work? Crescent Pain & Spine, Dr. Omar Haddad, is in network for member PSH-55017742. Is 05/15/2026 booked, one day after the Millbrook slot it replaces, with therapy carrying on in the evenings, so there's no new gap? Is the Millbrook slot off the calendar, with a reminder call on 05/13/2026 and an attendance check on 05/18/2026? Does every task have a date or an owner? And read your notes back for advice. Saying one place gives better care than the other fails, however kindly it's meant. Here's a little mystery to carry into the Knowledge Check. That 05/15/2026 injection is going to produce a bill, an EOB and, weeks later, a statement asking John for money. {name}, you've already seen how that story ends. Who remembers the number?
check.ask: {name}, if Crescent's first opening had been weeks away, who would you tell, and what would you ask them?

case.say: Game: Beat the Adjuster. I'm putting the adjuster's four arguments on the board: not serious, recovered early, treatment unnecessary, another cause. {name}, pick one and knock it down with a document, not a sentence. Good. Here's what landed on 06/22/2026. John Doe reached MMI on 06/12/2026, and Dr. Alana Reyes's Causation Letter of 06/19/2026 is in. She says delayed presentation is clinically consistent with a disc injury whose nerve symptoms build over days to weeks, and that the injury was more likely than not caused by the collision. In plain words: a late start to treatment makes medical sense for this injury. Atty. Thorne wants the Gap Explanation Record before the pre-demand session, with both interruptions at exact dates, every reason beside its dated document, “account only” where there isn't one, and a defense-eye pass first. And yes, there are two gaps. Last activity's mystery: the second one runs 04/02 to 04/21/2026.

Thorne through Tasks. {name}, you're building the 14-day band. {name}, you've got the 19-day band. Why so precise? You'll read Peach State's 06/03/2026 EOB for claim PS-2605-449021 line by line and say where each amount goes. You'll handle Crescent's 07/01/2026 statement asking John Doe for $1,540.00. Thorne involved before the appointment. {name}, you're our first contestant. {name}, you're the judge.

Riverton Spine & Rehab reports John Doe has missed two visits, he isn't answering anyone, and Dana Whitfield has asked John for a Recorded Statement. Tell me what you do first, second and third, and what each step protects. A couple of things I'll be looking for. I'll compare your self-rating with your score, and if there's a wide gap, we'll talk it through. One thing before you rate yourself: the line on legal advice works as a gate. I'm going to ask you, “Is this gap going to wreck my case?” If I hear “don't worry,” I ring the buzzer and {name} takes over. Ready? Good. Rewrite “Was it because you had no car?” so it surfaces the same reason without suggesting it, and explain what the leading version costs. And a tip from someone who's graded a lot of these: “see attached” is not an answer. Neither is a smiley face, which, yes, I've received.

summary.say: Time for your Self-Summary. Same date, 04/08/2026. Riverton Spine & Rehab says John Doe has missed two visits, he isn't answering anyone, and Dana Whitfield wants a Recorded Statement from him. What do you do first, second and third, and what does each step protect? While you're thinking about records, here's something to chew on. summary.ask: {name}, why is a provider's offer to change a record more dangerous than a note that's simply missing?

A five on everything tells me you're either a genius or you didn't read the list. But does the paperwork add up to the same number everywhere it appears? {name}, I bet one total on this file disagrees with itself somewhere.
scale.ask: {name}, which skill from today would you most want another run at in the simulator?

why.say: Pop quiz, no pressure, mostly. There's $7,965.00 in liens waiting behind a $10,000 BI limit. A lien is a bill that gets paid out of the settlement before the client sees his share, and BI is the at-fault driver's bodily injury coverage. Mental math, everyone: how much of that layer is left for John Doe? {name}, you're first. {name}, check that answer. Right, $2,035.00. Feel that number? That's why pre-demand matters. The demand goes out later today, but what it can claim gets decided right here. Pre-demand is where most of a file's value is won or lost, because the demand can only spend what this audit proves. One duplicate line or one unchecked limit is Keystone's easy out. And remember last block's mystery, the charge that shouldn't be there? It's hiding in one provider's statement. Keep your eyes open; I'll reveal it on the model slide.
why.ask: {name}, with $7,965.00 in liens behind a $10,000 BI limit, how much of that layer is left?

theory.say: Think of the pre-demand audit as the final stress test: the point where we stop collecting and start using, leaving the defense zero easy outs. It starts with what we call the trinity of case alignment. Fancy name, simple idea: the story, the physical evidence and the medical records all have to agree. If one's out of line, the value collapses. Maximum Medical Improvement, MMI, is the doctor's finding that he's as good as he's going to get. Once that happens, the bills are complete and the audit can begin. Special damages, or Specials, are the provable dollar loss: Medical Bills plus lost wages plus Property Damage, and every line needs a document. The medical and billing audit runs three passes: dates for gaps, billing codes for duplicates, and prior history for old injuries. {name}, quick guess before the next slide: which pass do you think catches the most money?
theory.ask: {name}, which of these audit ideas is new to you, and which part of John Doe's file would it test first?

theory2.say: Four more pieces. Liens and subrogation come first. Subrogation is just a payer's right to be paid back out of the recovery. Health Plans, government payers and LOP providers, who treated now and get paid later, may all claim repayment, and every lien shrinks his net. The Property Damage deep dive looks at the photos of where the car was hit, the estimate against the final bill and any supplements, because the car proves the force behind the injury. The defense-eye audit is reading the file the way the adjuster will: social media, a minor-impact label, the venue, which is where the case would be tried, and naming each value killer. And policy-limits targets are the verified limits in the order they open. That's what each policy can pay, which isn't the same thing as what the claim's worth. {name}, put your adjuster hat on for this one.
theory2.ask: {name}, what on John Doe's file would an adjuster point to for a minor-impact argument?

frame.say: This is the Master Audit Checklist, and I love a checklist. A pilot runs one before every flight, even after twenty years, and nobody calls the pilot lazy. The only lazy checklist is the one you tick from memory without opening the file. On the money side: Specials, meaning Medical Bills, lost wages and Property Damage, every line documented. Lost wages need the employer's wage letter plus a doctor's work note, and without both they usually get rejected. Then lien resolution, every payer who wants to be paid back. For liability proof: the final Police Report, witness contact and any drift in their statements, and whether the crash physics even works. The Property Damage deep dive checks the point of impact and any supplement showing hidden structural damage. And medical and billing gets the date check with every gap explained, the code check with no duplicates, and five to ten years of history. {name}, read the third line aloud for us.
frame.ask: {name}, which line of this checklist do you think is weakest on John Doe's file today?

rules.say: First question: who decides John reached MMI? Not you, and not John. It's Lakeside Orthopedics, recorded from its 06/12/2026 note with the future-care plan. Audit for verification, valuation, risk and compliance, with the SOL, the deadline to sue, of 02/06/2028 on the calendar. The Civic runs on its own Keystone PD claim, so his BI Specials are medical plus wages. Three passes: dates for the 14 days and the 19-day disruption, codes for duplicates, and prior history, the 2021 low-back visits. Show billed beside paid, because that choice is Atty. Thorne's. Northgate verifies 9 shifts at 8 hours and $22.00, so $1,584.00, and flag the five shifts with no note. The $3,400 to $6,800 in future injections stays out of the total. Register every lien, including Peach State's $1,860.00. $16,401.40 already exceeds the $10,000 limit. You audit, total and flag; you don't value the case. The lazy audit adds up the bills. The high-value audit proves every one.
rules.ask: {name}, who decides that John Doe reached MMI, and where do you record it from?

model.say: Here's the reveal. Read this one left to right. First there's a gate, MMI on 06/12/2026, with a green tick. Nothing enters the ledger until that's passed. In the centre is the ledger itself. And there's our mystery: the Riverton Spine & Rehab row. $6,290.00 is struck through in red and replaced by $6,105.00, with a badge flagging a $185.00 duplicate on 05/04/2026. One visit, billed twice. That's what the code check catches. Underneath is the sum, $14,817.40 in medicals plus $1,584.00 in wages, which gives $16,401.40. The future medical card sits outside the frame, in the story, not the total. On the right are the targets in the order they open: $10,000 BI, $20,000 Host UM and $10,000 Relative UM, each with its source. Quick translation: UM is the coverage that pays when the at-fault driver's insurance runs out, Host UM sits on the car John was riding in, and Relative UM sits on the policy of a relative he lives with. UM is uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage, which steps in when the at-fault driver's coverage isn't enough. {name}, the floor is yours.
model.ask: {name}, what would Keystone have done with that $185.00 duplicate if we hadn't caught it?

job.say: The story starts on 06/12/2026, when the MMI note arrives. You record MMI and the future-care plan on the treatment timeline and open the pre-demand audit as a task with an owner and a date. As the final bills and records come in, you build the Specials ledger and match it against the dates until every billed date matches a visit and the medical total is $14,817.40. Then you register every lien and record billed beside paid in the Liens tab and the Net Sheet's Lien Tracker, with the billed-versus-paid question routed to Atty. Thorne. Finally, before the ask, you re-verify each limit in the Coverage Matrix: $10,000, then $20,000, then $10,000, $40,000 in all, each with its written source. I once saw a demand go out citing a limit that had changed three weeks earlier. The adjuster's reply was one line long, and it was not a compliment. {name}, you're up.
job.ask: {name}, why re-verify the limits now, when the Coverage Matrix was confirmed weeks ago?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Clues one at a time; call Do or Don't and name the rule. {name}, you're keeping score. The good habits: stress-testing the file before the defense does, locking in total damages and protecting them by finding every lien before the demand, and recording the source of every figure so Atty. Thorne can check any line in seconds. The traps: sending the demand and hoping nobody checks the math, padding the Specials with future care, and finding a lien after the release is signed. That last one is like finding the receipt after you've returned the gift. Watch billed versus paid, too: show both and route the choice. Now your mystery for the next lesson. You've got all these numbers. Atty. Thorne has about ten seconds to read your first line. {name}, what's the one sentence you'd put at the top?
dodont.ask: {name}, why doesn't the Civic's repair ever count toward the $40,000 or the BI Specials?

why.say: Game: Ten-Second Boss. I'm Atty. Thorne, I've got a hearing in ten minutes, and I'll read exactly one line of your memo. Here are two first lines. One: “On 02/06/2026 John Doe was a front-seat passenger…” Two: “John Doe is at MMI with $16,401.40 in audited Specials against a $10,000 BI limit, and I need your decisions.” {name}, which one do I read before I walk out? Right, the second. And that's last block's mystery answered. He makes the strategy calls from your brief, so its shape matters. A brief that opens with the story buries the decision. One that hides a risk misleads him. And one that makes the call for him crosses a line that isn't yours to cross. We've all sat in a strategy meeting that could have been an email. Today you learn to write the email so good the meeting is fast.
why.ask: {name}, which of those two opening lines could Atty. Thorne act on in the first ten seconds?

theory.say: A pre-demand audit is the file's sanity check, and the strategy brief carries its findings, not conclusions, to Atty. Thorne, who makes every call. The brief reports on the four core audit objectives, which I'll reveal on the next slide. It flags statement drift, which is a witness whose story changes between tellings, because drift is an opening for the defense. It names the value killers the defense-eye audit turned up, like social media, a minor-impact label or the venue, and counsel weighs each one. And it always carries the lien totals, because when the math is wrong or a lien gets missed, you get a short-funded settlement. That's a settlement where, after everyone's paid back, the client takes home little or nothing. Imagine making that phone call. {name}, have you ever had to give someone news like that, at any job?
theory.ask: {name}, what would a short-funded settlement mean for John Doe, in plain terms?

frame.say: Here's the reveal: the four core objectives the brief rests on. Verification asks whether the facts match the physical evidence, meaning the photos, the Police Report and the scene. Valuation asks whether the damages are calculated right, with the bills, the wages and future care each backed by a document. Note, we calculate damages; Atty. Thorne decides what the case is worth. Risk assessment covers the weak spots the defense will argue: comparative negligence, which means blaming the client for part of the crash, social media, a minor-impact label, venue. And compliance means every legal requirement is met before the demand goes out, the Statute of Limitations first. If you can report a finding under each of the four, you're ready to brief. If you can't, you're not ready, no matter how nice the formatting is. {name}, give me one finding under verification from John Doe's file.
frame.ask: {name}, under which of these four objectives does John Doe's file still have an open question?

rules.say: Lead with the bottom line in one sentence: MMI 06/12/2026, $16,401.40 in audited Specials against a $10,000 BI limit, decisions needed before any demand is drafted. Next the facts, audited and sourced: report RPD-26-018842, Smith cited for failure to stop, Ruth Calloway checked for drift, and the doorbell video. On force, John's door was struck at about 28 mph, and the Civic went from $6,940.00 to $9,255.00 with a $2,315.00 A-pillar supplement. The A-pillar is the post of the car's frame beside the windshield, so a supplement there means the body shop found frame damage after the first estimate, and that tells an adjuster this crash had real force. Then the risks, each paired with its answering document. Here's the teaser: there's one risk almost every new Case Manager leaves out. {name}, guess. It's the 2021 low-back visits, and Keystone will find them. Then decisions as questions, and options with consequences. Record his decisions the same day. Saying Specials exceed the limit is a finding; “we should demand limits” is his call. The lazy brief hides the bad news. The high-value brief brings it first, with the answer stapled on.
rules.ask: {name}, which risk would you be tempted to leave out of the brief, and what happens when Keystone finds it first?

model.say: Here's the brief, laid out in the order counsel reads it. It's one page. One. Not the whole file printed “just in case,” which I've seen, and which arrived on Atty. Thorne's desk with a binder clip that gave up halfway. Five bands. First, the bottom line, in navy, one line, the biggest type on the page. Second, the audited facts, split into narrative, physicality and medicals, each with a green tick. Third, the risks, in red: the 14-Day Gap, the disruption, the 2021 low back and that “degenerative” read, each tied to the document that answers it. Fourth, the decisions needed, every item written as a question. Fifth, the options with their consequences. And down the right edge runs a rail that says Atty. Elijah Thorne decides, ending in a dated, tasked decision record. {name}, why do you think the decisions are questions?
model.ask: {name}, why is every item in the decisions band written as a question rather than a recommendation?

job.say: So the audit's complete. You draft the one-page memo and the exhibit index, the numbered list of every attached document, in the Action Plan Editor, five sections in order, every exhibit label matching its page. Once it's ready, you book the strategy session on the CMS calendar and send the memo ahead through the Email Workspace, and the session happens before any demand is drafted. After the session, you record each decision in counsel's own words in Case Notes and open its tasks, each one dated, attributed to Atty. Thorne, with an owner and a due date. And since those decisions change the plan, you mark the Case Plan superseded, meaning replaced, and re-route the new version the same day. Why so strict? Because six months from now, if anyone asks why we demanded what we demanded, the answer is in the file, in his words, with a date. {name}, that protects you too.
job.ask: {name}, why re-route the Case Plan as a new version instead of just editing the old one?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Three clues, one at a time; call Do or Don't and name the rule. {name}, first buzz is yours. On the good side: you bring the bad facts yourself, so counsel never meets a risk first in the adjuster's letter. You find discrepancies before the defense does. You check John's public social media, and you never suggest deleting a post. You use the structural supplement to answer a minor-impact label, and you leave venue to Atty. Thorne. On the trap side: a three-page memo, an exhibit index with mismatched page numbers, and briefing the first PD estimate instead of the final figure. And watch the recommend line: “email the demand and log her acknowledgement” is operations; “we should demand limits” isn't yours. Now your mystery. The demand goes to Keystone with a deadline attached. {name}, what's the one thing that has to be on the calendar the second it's sent?
dodont.ask: {name}, is “email it to the adjuster and log her written acknowledgement” a recommendation you're allowed to make?

case.say: This landed on 07/01/2026: billing complete, Special Damages Audit due, LSH-2026-MVA-770412. Lakeside Orthopedics declared MMI on 06/12/2026, and Dr. Reyes's Causation Letter arrived 06/19/2026. Every bill's in. Riverton Urgent Care at $685.00, Riverton Spine & Rehab's statement of 34 lines at $185.00, or $6,290.00, with its visit notes, three Lakeside Orthopedics visits at $640.00, Summit Imaging at $2,395.00, Crescent Pain & Spine at $3,400.00, which Peach State paid $1,860.00 on, and Riverton Drug at $312.40. Northgate's HR letter of 06/30/2026 verifies 9 missed shifts at 8 hours times $22.00. I'm handing you the bills, not the totals. Teaser: there's one number in that list that doesn't add up, and you already know which provider it's hiding in. {name}, don't say it yet. Let your group find it.
case.ask: {name}, before you total Riverton Spine & Rehab's statement, how many visits do its notes actually show?

task.say: You'll build John Doe's audited Specials ledger in the CMS Financial Ledger. Enter each provider's charges with dates, the billed amount and who paid. Match Riverton Spine & Rehab's lines against its visit notes, and take out any line no visit supports. Total the medical, add the verified wages and show billed beside paid, meaning what the provider charged next to what was actually paid. Future medical goes in the narrative, not the ledger. List every lien with its amount in Liens and the Lien Tracker, and re-verify the three policy-limits targets in order on the Insurance tab. {name}, you're on medical lines. {name}, wages and liens. Part of your grade is what you flag rather than decide. The lazy ledger copies the totals off the statements. The high-value ledger proves every line. And “I was busy, so I trusted the statement” is exactly the sentence Keystone is hoping you'll say.
task.ask: {name}, Peach State paid $1,860.00 on a $3,400.00 bill. Which number goes in the demand?

check.say: Check your ledger to the cent. Riverton Spine & Rehab's notes show 33 visits against 34 lines, so the 05/04/2026 duplicate comes out and $6,290.00 becomes $6,105.00, with a corrected statement requested. Your medical total should be $14,817.40, down from $15,002.40. Wages are 9 shifts at 8 hours and $22.00, so $1,584.00, which gives total Specials of $16,401.40. {name}, read me your number. If it's anything else, a line is wrong. Here's the subtle one. Five of those nine shifts, 02/09 to 02/13/2026, fall before any provider saw John. Flag them with Northgate's Attendance Record; never drop them. Billed sits beside paid, and the choice goes to Atty. Thorne. Future medical stays in the narrative, and the targets run $10,000, $20,000, $10,000. Your mystery: Atty. Thorne will push on three weak spots in the strategy session. {name}, name them before he does.
check.ask: {name}, why flag those five early shifts instead of quietly dropping them from the wage claim?

case.say: It's 07/08/2026, and this is Atty. Thorne's note. He's read your audit, and the strategy session on John Doe is today at 2:00 p.m. in his office. Bottom line first, he says. Expect him to push the way Keystone will, on low speed, the 14 days and the “degenerative” read, which is the argument that John's neck was just wearing out with age. Bring the facts, the documents and the operational options, and remember the decisions on the demand are his. Your audit's done: MMI 06/12/2026, Specials of $16,401.40, liens of $1,860.00 and $6,105.00, and targets of $10,000 BI, $20,000 Host UM and $10,000 Relative UM. And there's your answer to last activity's mystery: low speed, the gap, and degenerative. Fair warning, he'll interrupt you inside the first minute. This is not the meeting that could have been an email. This is the meeting your email made possible. {name}, ready?
case.ask: {name}, if he says “Keystone will call this low-speed,” what objective fact do you answer with first?

task.say: You'll run the pre-demand strategy session with AI Atty. Elijah Thorne in the Call Simulator. Brief him in order. Start with the bottom line, MMI, $16,401.40 in Specials and the $10,000 BI limit, then the audited facts, the risks with their answering documents, the decisions he has to make, and the operational consequences of each option. Meet every challenge with dated documents, not adjectives; “it was a serious crash” doesn't answer anything. Recommend only on operations, and get his decisions on the demand, the gap, the UM consents and billed versus paid. Read each decision back before you close. Afterwards, record them in Case Notes, open a task for each in Tasks, and re-route the Case Plan. {name}, you're in the chair first. {name}, {name}, you're observers, and you're writing down his decisions word for word. These decisions drive the demand, and the demand drives the offer.
task.ask: {name}, as an observer, what did Atty. Thorne decide, in his own words?

check.say: Grade your decision record, not the conversation. If a decision isn't dated, attributed and tasked, the session didn't happen. Did you lead with the bottom line, figures exact? Did you meet the low-speed challenge with objective facts: Smith running the stop sign and getting cited, John's door struck at about 28 mph, the $2,315.00 A-pillar supplement, and the C5-C6 herniation, a slipped disc in the neck, on the 03/13/2026 MRI? Remember, that's the extra repair bill for the frame post beside the windshield: proof of force. Did you meet the gap with documents rather than an apology, and raise the 2021 visits and the “degenerative” read unprompted? His decisions should be recorded: the time-limited BI demand to Dana Whitfield, served 07/20/2026, the gap addressed up front, the UM consent plan, and billed versus paid. And when he asked what you think we should demand, did you hand the figure back? {name}, did you? Your mystery: a Time-Limited Demand has a clock. That's a demand with a deadline built in: the insurance company has to say yes inside a set window or the offer goes away, like a coupon that expires at midnight. {name}, what happens on the file the day it runs out?
check.ask: {name}, when AI Atty. Thorne asked what you'd demand, what exactly did you say back?

questions.say: Look at the gate bar. This module turns the last two chips green: Specials audited at $16,401.40, and strategy approved by Atty. Thorne. The demand doesn't go out until all six are green. Quick warm-up game before you write: Price Is Right, audit edition. I'll name a number from the file, and you shout higher or lower than what it should be. Riverton Spine & Rehab, $6,290.00? {name}? Right, lower: $6,105.00. That's the answer to the last mystery. Now answer from this file, in your own words. Total John Doe's Specials from the bills, showing the Riverton correction, the medical total, the wage math and the final figure. Say who decides MMI, when John Doe's was, why the demand waits for it, and where the $3,400 to $6,800 in future medical goes. And name the four audit objectives, with one finding each on this file.
questions.ask: {name}, which two chips on the gate bar does this module turn green?

summary.say: Now your Self-Summary, in your own words. The scenario takes us back to 04/08/2026. Riverton Spine & Rehab reports two missed visits, Keystone ended Margaret's rental on 03/19, his carpool ended 04/01, and Dana Whitfield has asked him for a Recorded Statement. Tell me what you do first, second and third, and what each one protects. And while you write, picture this. You find an error in an exhibit the day before the 07/20/2026 service date. The lazy move is to send it anyway and fix it later. The high-value move is to stop the package, fix every total that cites it, and tell Atty. Thorne before anything goes out. Serving a known error to make the date is the failure, because once Keystone has the wrong number, it's their favorite number. {name}, have you ever hit send and then seen the typo?
summary.ask: {name}, which number on this file would you defend line by line to Dana Whitfield, and where does every cent come from?

scale.say: And to close out the pre-demand audit, your Skill Scale. Rate each skill from one to five and submit it for review. I'll put your self-rating beside your score, and where they're far apart, we'll sit down and talk it through. Be especially honest on the billed-versus-paid question. If any of your answers picked a column for the demand, that loses the UPL marks, however good the rest of the work was. Now your mystery. The audited figure is $16,401.40, and the BI limit is $10,000. The demand is going to ask for one specific number. {name}, without telling me what it should be, because that's Atty. Thorne's call, tell me where on the file you'd look to find out what he decided.
scale.ask: {name}, looking back over the pre-demand audit, which skill feels most solid to you now?

why.say: Quick game: finish the sentence. "An IOU is…" {name}, go. {name}, give me yours. Good, because today's star is the most official IOU you'll ever see. John Doe needs chiropractic care next week, and nothing he has will pay for it. That's where a Letter of Protection comes in. In plain English, it's a written promise that the provider gets paid out of the settlement, so he can be treated now instead of waiting. It keeps care moving, and care that keeps moving keeps the file honest, with no gaps for an adjuster to point at. But here's the twist, and it's the one clients never believe: it isn't free money. It's a balance against his recovery, and he still owes it. So we track it from the day it's signed.
why.ask: {name}, if the settlement came in lower than the bills, who would still owe the provider?

doc.say: Before you prepare or file one, let's open up the Letter of Protection, or LOP. {name}, quick guess: is it insurance? Hands up for yes. Put them down, it isn't. It's the firm's signed promise that a provider's reasonable charges will be paid from any recovery, so treatment can start now. Its legal purpose is to keep care going when no payer applies: the provider defers collection, meaning it waits to get paid, and in return its charges are protected from the settlement, judgment or verdict. Its evidentiary role, the job it does as proof, is to fix the lien. Riverton Spine & Rehab's letter, acknowledged on 02/23/2026, is why its charges come out of John Doe's recovery, and it says plainly that he stays responsible whether or not there is one. Your handling is to check every payer first, get it signed before the first visit, request the ledger every 30 days, and leave its meaning to Atty. Thorne. The lazy version sends the LOP and forgets it. The high-value version checks the ledger every month, because a surprise balance at settlement is money straight out of John's pocket. An LOP is a pinky promise with a signature, and providers remember every pinky.
doc.ask: {name}, why does the letter say John Doe stays responsible even if there's no recovery?

rules.say: Here's how we handle it. First, an LOP is the last resort, so we check health insurance, MedPay and PIP before anything else and write down why none of them works. Second, it gets signed before the first visit and filed. Riverton's was signed on 02/23/2026. Third, we ask for the itemized ledger every thirty days and update the Liens tab, so the balance never surprises anyone. And when John Doe asks where to go, we give him options with the facts, book the one he picks, and log his choice in his own words. The lazy version is "Sure, go to the place down the street, I'll send them a letter." The high-value version is a payer check on file, a signed LOP before visit one, and a ledger that's never more than thirty days old. I once met a client who thought "Letter of Protection" meant he had a bodyguard now. He was a little disappointed. {name}, your turn.
rules.ask: {name}, why does it matter that John Doe picks the provider, and not us?

job.say: On the job it looks like this. When no payer covers the care, you document the payer check and route the LOP to Atty. Thorne to approve. When it's signed, you file it and set the recurring ledger task. And when John Doe asks where he should go, you hand him two or three options with their locations, hours and network status, tell him about any relationship the firm has with them, and book his choice. What you never say is which one is better for his case. That's the line. Why it matters: at settlement, every LOP dollar comes off the top of John's check unless someone negotiates it down, and a clean ledger is what we negotiate with. Now a mystery for the next lesson. John Doe is spending money on this crash every single week, and none of it shows up on any provider's bill. {name}, what is it, and who's writing it down?
job.ask: {name}, a provider asks you to promise they'll be paid in full. What do you say instead?

theory.say: Four ideas carry this lesson, and {name}, I'll ask you to rank them when I'm done. A Letter of Protection is a written promise to pay a provider from the settlement, so it's a claim against John Doe's recovery, not insurance. Payer-first means we check health insurance, MedPay and PIP before we ever reach for one. The LOP balance grows with every visit, so the itemized ledger every thirty days keeps the Liens tab honest. And referrals are options and logistics only: a list, the network status, the booking, and his choice. Think of an LOP like a tab at a restaurant. It's great to eat now and pay later, right up until the check comes and nobody remembers ordering dessert eleven times. The ledger is how we remember.
theory.ask: {name}, which of these four would you check first on a new provider bill?

why.say: Guessing game. {name}, guess how much it costs John Doe, out of his own pocket, to get to therapy three times a week for a month. Rides, gas, parking, the copay. Shout a number. {name}, higher or lower? Here's the point. Picture John Doe's week once the rental's gone. He still has therapy three times a week. Somebody drives him, or he pays for a ride. There's a prescription, maybe a brace. None of that shows up on a provider's bill, but every dollar of it is a cost of the crash. And here's the catch: it's recoverable only if somebody wrote it down when it happened. That somebody is you. Copays are sneaky that way. Ten dollars here, twenty-five there, and by month three it's a car payment nobody tracked. You keep the log; what the demand claims, and at what rate, is Atty. Thorne's call under the governing state's rules.
why.ask: {name}, what costs do you think John Doe is paying out of his own pocket right now?

theory.say: Four ideas. Out-of-pocket costs are the client's own money spent because of the crash: mileage, rides, parking, prescriptions, copays, equipment, and any rental the owner paid, each with its receipt. The trip log is the date, the provider and the round-trip miles for every visit, kept from the first appointment, never rebuilt from memory. The mileage rate is whatever the governing state's rules allow, and Atty. Thorne confirms it; for reference, when this course was written the IRS rates were twenty and a half cents a mile medical and seventy-two and a half business. Rental reimbursement: days past the cutoff or a rate above the cap are the owner's cost, sent with the Property Damage claim. And every cost goes into the Specials ledger, our list of money damages, the day its receipt arrives. The lazy trip log gets written the week before the demand: "uh, I think I went to therapy a lot?" The high-value one is boring, dated and bulletproof. {name}, which one would you rather defend?
theory.ask: {name}, why does a trip log kept as treatment happens beat a list rebuilt at the demand?

rules.say: Here are the rules. Out-of-pocket costs are Specials, and each one needs its receipt or its log. Start the trip log at the first visit: date, provider, round-trip miles. The rate comes from the governing state's rules, confirmed by Atty. Thorne. A rental the carrier didn't pay is the owner's cost; keep the receipt and send it with the Property Damage claim. When the rental ends, transport becomes a barrier to care, so plan the rides before a visit is missed. Check every payer first, so nothing is claimed twice. Enter each cost the day its receipt arrives, then total the log and route it to Atty. Thorne before the demand. And never promise the client he'll be repaid. True story: a client once brought me his receipts in a shoebox. Not sorted, not dated, and one of them was for a hot dog. We kept the parking receipts. We did not claim the hot dog.
rules.ask: {name}, John Doe asks if he'll get his ride money back. What can you say without giving legal advice?

job.say: On the job, it runs like this. Treatment starts, so you open the trip log in Case Notes, set a task, and tell John Doe exactly what to keep: every receipt, and every trip with its date, office and miles. When a receipt comes in, you enter the cost in the Financial Ledger under Specials the same day and file the receipt in Documents. When MMI is reached, meaning the doctor says he's as good as he's going to get, and the demand is next, you total the log and route it to Atty. Thorne, who confirms the rate and decides what the demand claims. Small numbers, big outcome: a few hundred dollars of documented mileage also proves John showed up, visit after visit, and that's worth far more at the negotiating table than the mileage itself. Now your mystery. Keystone ended Margaret's rental on 03/19/2026, and John's rides are now held together by a carpool. {name}, look at the file and predict the week his therapy is in danger.
job.ask: {name}, what's the one thing you'd tell John Doe to start keeping today?

why.say: Would you rather: spend $5,000 on one big bill nobody will ever discount, or on twelve small bills that might get discounted later? {name}, pick one. {name}, argue the other side. Hold that thought. Here's the thing about PIP: you only get to spend it once. Harbor Point's $5,000 paid five of John Doe's bills, and every dollar of it was a bill his settlement will never have to pay back. But where those dollars landed decided what was left for Peach State, for the Letter of Protection, and in the end for John's net, his take-home. The same ledger tells a BI adjuster, the one handling the at-fault driver's injury coverage, how serious the case looks, and in some states whether the defendant gets a credit for it. And last lesson's mystery, the $1,267.20 in wages? The bills used up the whole limit first. So the Case Manager who forecasts the limit, checks for anything that caps it and keeps the ledger exact is protecting the client's net months before anyone writes a demand.
why.ask: {name}, if PIP had paid twelve chiropractic visits instead of Summit's MRI, what would John Doe's file look like now?

rules.say: Here's the strategy in plain words, and the answer to the would-you-rather. On a typical file, PIP does the most good on the fixed costs, like the ER, imaging and specialist visits, because hospitals rarely reduce at the end and LOP providers often will. John's file shows it: PIP paid urgent care, Lakeside three times and Summit's $2,395.00 MRI, while chiropractic and therapy ran under the LOP. Your part is the forecast, not the choice; routing outside the Payer Order is Atty. Thorne's call. The limit is shared, so the bills used it by 06/26/2026 and the $1,267.20 wage benefit was never paid. In states with an EMC rule, meaning PIP can be capped unless a doctor documents an emergency medical condition, you check the records early and never ask a doctor to make that finding. Where set-off applies, the defendant gets credit for PIP paid, like a gift card taken off the bill. Riverton is add-on, meaning PIP is a bonus on top, so it doesn't reduce BI, the other driver's coverage, or UM, the underinsured coverage that kicks in after it. The lazy Case Manager pays bills as they arrive. The high-value one sees the empty tank coming.
rules.ask: {name}, John Doe's PIP took four months to run out. Does that mean his case is minor, and what figure tells the real story?

job.say: Three moments on the job. When a PIP check clears, you post it in the PIP Log and record what's left, what's still coming and the wage claim, so you see the empty date before it arrives. When a bill could go to PIP or to an LOP, you lay out both routes with the figures in an email to Atty. Thorne and log his decision; you never re-route a claim another payer already paid. And on a file in an EMC state, when the first treating records arrive, you check the rule and look for the finding. If it's missing, Atty. Thorne hears about it that day. Quick war story. A Case Manager I trained once found out a client's PIP was empty from a cheerful letter that said, "Benefits exhausted! Have a wonderful day!" Three bills had already bounced. Don't let a form letter tell you news your ledger should have told you weeks ago. Now the mystery: there's a piece of paper that lets John Doe get treated now and pay later. {name}, before the next lesson, guess what it costs him.
job.ask: {name}, what's the first thing you record when a PIP check clears, and why that one?

why.say: By now John Doe's treatment is under way, and three money questions sit on his file at once. Who pays each bill while the claim is open? Who's going to want paying back out of the recovery? And what has to be flagged in the CMS right now, before anyone argues about it? This lesson puts all three on one page. Every card has more behind it, and I want you to be able to say the two flag rules word for word by the end, because a lien found at disbursement or a gap nobody recorded is how a good file loses money.
why.ask: {name}, which of those three questions do you think gets missed most often, and why?

theory.say: Four cards, and each one opens. Every coverage gets sorted twice, whose it is and what it pays, and only BI, Host UM and Relative UM make the $40,000 stack. The Payer-First Principle sends each bill to Harbor Point PIP first, then Peach State, then an LOP last. Health subrogation means the plan claims back only what it paid, for the collision's care: Peach State asserted $3,618.00 on 06/10/2026 and confirmed $1,860.00 in writing on 06/24/2026. And the two CMS flags go up the day you know, in facts only, and get routed to Atty. Thorne.
theory.ask: {name}, before I open the last card, what's the exact day the lien flag goes up?

rules.say: Here are the rules in the course's own words. Only BI and UM stack, and that's $40,000; PIP and PD sit outside it. Bills go PIP, then Peach State, then an LOP. The lien is flagged in CMS Liens on first notice, which on this file was Peach State's letter of 02/27/2026, and always before any demand is drafted. The gap is flagged the day the records show it: 02/06/2026 to 02/20/2026 is 14 days, counted exactly, recorded as facts, routed, with a watch for any later break. Neither flag is a judgment. Whether a lien is enforceable or what a gap does to value belongs to Atty. Thorne.

job.say: On the job it comes down to three triggers. A reimbursement right is first noticed, so you flag the lien in CMS Liens with its identifiers, dated before any demand. The plan's itemized ledger arrives, so you audit each line, dispute what isn't the collision's care in writing, and change the register only when the plan confirms the figure, here $1,860.00. And the records show first care on 02/20/2026, so you flag the 14-Day Gap in the Action Plan Editor's risks band in facts only, route it, and keep watching, which is how the 19-day break in April was caught the day the alert came in.
job.ask: {name}, what would you write in the risks band, word for word?

case.say: It's 06/22/2026, ten days after Lakeside declared MMI. John Doe signed Northgate Distribution's employee authorization this morning. What we have on his wages is a draft worksheet somebody built from his own account over the phone, and it claims $1,760.00. Nothing in it comes from a record yet. Angela Ruiz runs HR at Northgate, and the Special Damages Audit is due on 07/01/2026. Every missed shift that reaches the demand has to stand up to an adjuster who will check it against payroll and the medical chart.
case.ask: {name}, looking at that worksheet, what in it came from a record?

task.say: First you write the Employer Verification email to Angela Ruiz in the Email Workspace, with the authorization: the Wage Loss Verification Form, payroll records and his W-2, and the employer's confirmation of his rate, his shift hours, each missed date, any overtime and the physical demands of the job. When she replies, she'll ask for his MRI and whether the settlement repays him, and your answer sends no records and says nothing about the claim. Then you match every missed shift to a provider record, flag the five February shifts to Atty. Thorne, audit the draft to the verified total, and enter it in the Specials and the Net Sheet.
task.ask: {name}, why does the authorization not let you send Northgate his MRI?

audit.say: Now call every row of the draft against Northgate's records and the doctors' notes. You'll find 02/18 and 02/19 claimed, and he worked both. The MRI is written as 03/12, and it was 03/13. The 05/18 shift rests on his memory, when Crescent's work note covers 05/15 through 05/18. Light duty and overtime appear that Northgate says never happened. And the five call-outs from 02/09 to 02/13 were simply left out because there's no doctor's note. Those stay in, flagged, never dropped. Northgate answered in minutes here; a real employer can take weeks, which is why the request goes out the day MMI is declared.
audit.ask: {name}, why is dropping the February shifts worse than claiming them with a flag?

check.say: Check your work before you hand it in. Northgate confirmed the rate, the hours, no overtime and the job's demands: lifting to 50 pounds, forklift, on his feet all shift. The 03/05, 03/13, 05/15 and 05/18 shifts are each matched to a provider record. The 02/09 to 02/13 shifts are kept and flagged with the call-out record, the EMS report and the 02/07 receipt. The draft went from $1,760.00 to $1,584.00, nine shifts at eight hours and $22.00. And not one page of his medical records went to his employer.
check.ask: {name}, if Keystone asked how you know he missed 03/13, what would you show them?

why.say: Here's the thing about coverage: it only tells you there's money. Whether anyone has to pay it is a different question, and that's liability. John Doe's file has three coverage layers, but none of them pays a cent unless Robert Smith is legally responsible. And the evidence that proves it is freshest right now. Ruth Calloway's memory fades, Margaret Doe's doorbell camera records over itself, and the Escape's data recorder goes wherever the car goes. So we investigate liability at claim set-up, right beside coverage, not at the demand.
why.ask: Which piece of John Doe's liability evidence would you lose first if nobody did anything this week?

rules.say: Start with the Police Report, RPD-26-018842, and read every field, not just the citation. Officer Garner cited Smith for failure to stop, and he named a witness, Ruth Calloway, who signed a statement on scene. The report also lists the Escape as a 2021, while Harbor Point's Declaration Page says 2020, so you record both and correct our record from the policy. Then preserve: the doorbell copy was secured on 02/19/2026 with its hash logged, and the data recorder needs a preservation request Atty. Thorne signs. And remember, Keystone accepting PD liability on Margaret's Civic doesn't bind its BI adjuster on John's claim.
rules.ask: The defense says John Doe wasn't wearing his belt. What on the file already answers that?

job.say: Three moments on the job. When claim set-up opens, you request the Police Report and read it field by field, logging the citation and the witness in the CMS. When you learn that video or vehicle data exists, you draft the preservation requests for Atty. Thorne's signature and log the chain of custody once a copy is secured. And whenever a carrier states its liability position, you record it in the Insurance tab with its date and its source, one carrier at a time.

why.say: Picture Atty. Thorne between two hearings with forty emails open. The ones that start with a story make him read to the end to find out what he's being asked, and the question found last gets answered last. So we flip it. Every note, email and brief to him opens with the decision or the action needed, and its deadline. Then why, then the facts, then what happens after each answer. It sounds small, but it's the difference between a yes by lunchtime and a deadline that slips past while the note waits.
why.ask: Think of the last long email you received. How far did you read before you knew what was being asked?

rules.say: The first line is the decision and its deadline, and the subject line carries it too. Something like: decision needed by 03/12/2026, approve declining Summit Imaging's LOP request, because the MRI goes to Harbor Point PIP, which applies first and still has $3,675.00 left. Then the facts with their sources, then the options: if yes, you send the decline and route the bill today; if no, you draft the LOP for his signature. One decision per note. And once he answers, you log the note and his answer in the CMS that same day and carry it out.
rules.ask: Your note holds two decisions with different deadlines. How do you send it so neither one is missed?

theory.say: Four ideas, and the first one carries the rest. An affidavit is a written statement of facts, sworn under oath before a notary, by someone who knows them first-hand. It ends in a jurat, “sworn to and subscribed before me,” and a false one is perjury. That's why it's proof and a letter isn't. Then three families on our file. Coverage: Robert Smith swears he has no other insurance, and John, if a carrier asks, swears he lives with Margaret and owns no car. Damages: each provider's records custodian swears the bills and records are true copies, and Northgate verifies the wages. And court: the process server swears Smith was served, which starts his answer clock.

why.say: {name}, here's a test. Keystone's adjuster writes to say Robert Smith has no other insurance. Would you settle at the $10,000 limit on that letter? I wouldn't, and neither will Harbor Point or Cardinal State. A letter is somebody's word. An affidavit is somebody's word under oath, from the person who actually knows: Smith himself, sworn on 08/10/2026. Every fact this file leans on, the coverage, John's residency, the bills, service on Smith, is only as strong as the paper that proves it. Get the sworn version and nobody can wave it away.
why.ask: Which fact on John Doe's file would hurt most if we could only assert it, not prove it?

rules.say: The rules are about who and what. Smith swears the affidavit of no other insurance; it's a condition of settling at the limit. John swears residency and no owned vehicle only if a carrier asks, and only from a draft Atty. Thorne has reviewed. Every certified records request asks for the custodian's affidavit in the same letter, because that's how the bills get into evidence without calling each provider. Northgate's wage letter proves the $1,584.00, sworn later if we sue. The process server's affidavit of service gets filed, 10/16/2026 on our file. And every affidavit gets checked before anyone relies on it: the affiant, the numbers, the dates, the signature, the jurat and the seal. A defect goes back to the sender. You never sign, notarize or fix someone else's sworn words.

job.say: On the job it comes down to three moments. When Atty. Thorne approves a demand at the limit, you request Smith's affidavit through Keystone and docket it; ours came back sworn on 08/10/2026. When a records request goes out, the custodian's affidavit is in the same request, so the set comes back ready for evidence. And when any affidavit arrives, you check it against the file, route a defect with a task, and file it where it'll be used: the demand conditions, the UM packages, the trial binder.
